"I think this falls on the teacher.  Someone spoke to this above... because if you have a teacher that is just terrible and doesn't know how to manage a class of mixed ability, you get very bored \gifted\"" students.  However, if the teacher knows how to differentiate properly, they can challenge your child, within the same confines of the concept being learned, at a deeper level.  Not just making your child do MORE work... but have your child do DIFFERENT work around the same topic.  Sometimes that can be as easy as asking one question to take it deeper.  The problem I've seen with this, however, is that sometimes those \""gifted\"" students still know in their head that they are getting different work.  They still think that they're smarter than the other kids, so they will tend to call the class boring.  Even though the teacher is definitely challenging the kid.  I've heard kids say, \""this class is easy\"" when I KNOW I have challenged them with difficult questions on a daily basis that they struggle with.  I had a girl tell me my Honors Geometry class (as an 8th grader) was easy.  I laughed... I said, \""This class isn't EASY!  You just got an A on a High School Geometry Honors Mid-Term.  That's hard to do!  It's not easy... I watch you work HARD every day!  I see you thinking... I see you struggle... I watch you debate... This is work!   And you work hard!  Just because you got an A, doesn't mean it's easy."""	1	0	0	5	2	3	Education	51e82854e8a51212000000af	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	D8FF02712FD0493D607B06A36F82494E	7/18/2013 17:39	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51e74f7de8a5120e0000001f	20

"This year, you may have a different experience than you have had in math class previously.  I am interested in your thinking and your learning.  I WILL give you problems that do not have just one way to be solved.  They WILL be difficult at times.  I expect you to put forth effort to try them, but I do NOT expect that you will get the right answer or even an answer at times.  The class will be about learning what we can from these difficult problems and our mistakes in order to make progress in our learning. I will not tell you a procedure for these problems.  Instead, I will be here to encourage you, ask you lots and lots of questions and learn along with you. None of us knows it all, and none of us will be the end of the year together.  I expect to learn about your thinking and hopefully some math as well. You should expect to learn about math but also about your own thinking. If you are putting forth effort and making progress, that is what will be valued instead of the number of questions right and wrong!"	1	0	0	4	3	3	Education	523c75a12911a80e00000039	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	1ED3851E985061C1EDC9295A0DD84296	9/20/2013 16:19	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	523c68da4921951600000005	4

"One thing the number cards do that I didn't see mentioned in the first few posts below is that they visually reinforce the idea that numbers can be broken up in many different ways. The discussion of the different ways people viewed the dots opens avenues for others to begin to consider how many different decompositions there are, and that these decompositions lead to many different arithmetic computations. Finally, the visual aspect of the exercise leaves a lasting impression almost like a puzzle that people might carry in the back of their minds as a reminder to think about numbers in different and use the relationships of the sub-parts to understand the numbers more deeply."	1	0	0	4.5	2.5	3	Education	523dae61e11ed8160000002b	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	CDD91978D849406D65444E67CFD04DE1	9/21/2013 14:34	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	2

"Have you tried using any specific study team strategies? For instance, I have seen teacher get great results using team roles, as artificial as they are. One idea is to give each student within a team a name tag that on one side, says their role. Task Manager, Recorder/reporter, Resource Manager, Facilitator. Then on the other side, you list sample questions the student in that role might ask. And you enforce it! You have a participation quiz where you tell the students \Today I'm going to be assessing how well you work as a team, and in particular, I will be looking at how well you perform in your role.\"" This sets the expectation that you want students to ALL be involved, not just some of them. "Are sit-down math problems during the summer the best way to help him overcome his math phobia? When I was seven, and my sister five, we had a computer game : Math Rabbit. We wanted to win all the prizes in the virtual carnival, so we would wake up on Saturday mornings, get on the MS Dos computer, and play for hours. Hardcore gaming wasn't a term back then, but that's what we would do with that silly carnival math game. It wasn't mom telling us to turn up the difficulty to Level 3 or Level 4, it was just us playing at a level we felt was easy enough to be fun, at the games we felt were fun.And that fun is way more useful than being able to borrow correctly at age 8. There's always age 9 for borrowing correctly, but he won't learn it then either if he's still afraid of math. Rereading this, it reminds me of an analogy to books - yes, your 8 year old CAN read challenging 3rd grade texts, but isn't it preferable if he's reading the easy Magic Treehouse series for hours and hours rather than crying at reading a page of a thick chapter book? Reading the easy books for hours will cause him to spurt in reading level so that before you know it, he's bringing home the Hobbit and Harry Potter book 7 to read because they look just as interesting as those \kiddy\"" books he practiced reading on.]Seriously, find an online game that's below his grade level and let him play it to give him repeated opportunities of doing math problems correctly and feeling that the problems (and thus math in general) is \""easy.\"" I have seventh graders on IXL who sometimes sneak and do all the 1st grade problems just because it is a confidence boost to score a 100%, even if it's for the skill Adding 1 - 10. Khan Academy is free and has these leveled-type problems too (though that site can be a pain to navigate).Alternatively, sit down with a deck of cards (1 - 10 only, Aces being 1) and play Addition War with him, so that he sees that math with mom can sometimes take the form of a game. "In my department students have been sitting in groups for over fifteen years.  I remember when it first started and it did take the students awhile to adjust to the idea.  They were distracted easily and off task, but they did adapt to the new environment.  I spent a great deal of time walking around the room and refocusing students and keeping them on task.  It got easier every year.  I cannot imagine ever going back to desks in rows!  I came up with a better way to form my groups this year. Method:With the help of peers, I compiled of list of thinking strengths that we believe are useful for learning math.  (Also in life)  Students were asked to put a plus in front of the two they thought were their strongest ones and a minus in front of their weakest one.Rationale:  1.	I wanted my students to think about their talents and areas in which they can grow this year.  This is a step in developing metacognition.  2.	Students think math is about getting the right answer and I wanted them to know other abilities are also important. Follow Up:1.	After they finished, I asked which thinking strength might bring the most success.  I used this opportunity to share the following ideas with my classes.   I believe the ability to ™think about mistakes and learn from themš is the most useful skill on the list.  I talked about the value of errors and how mistakes cause your brain to grow.  When you make a mistake, research says your brain develops new synapses.  I hope to challenge them so that they can learn from each other®s errors.  I explained that my goals for the year are to develop their thinking and communication skills.2.	I used their responses to form my groups by considering grade, sex and thinking strengths.  I constructed groups so each one reflected a variety of thinking strengths.        I also teach a traditional curriculum.  I cannot do inquiry based, but I discovered that you can make a small change that makes a big difference.  All you have to do is change WHEN you ask a question.  Ask a question you would normally ask, before the lesson and try to find one that has multiple entry points or several ways to solve it.  Let the students struggle and discuss and you answer questions.  The lesson comes from students presenting their work.  Afterwards as a class you organize their methods and fill in any gaps.  I usually try to find a couple more problems that are different but involve the same concepts. "I have a high proportion of perfectionist students in my class, so I have developed several ongoing procedures to model learning from mistakes, and to put mistakes in learning perspective. When I call on students attempting to answer a challenging question (and sometimes I cold call), I will sometimes make explicit that I am checking for understanding, or trying to evaluate where students are now in their thinking. Because it works for me, I also rhetorically ask \will the floor open and swallow him if he's wrong?\"" or \""will anyone die if she makes a mistake?\"" In addition, especially during math, I remind them to be watching carefully because I make frequent mistakes, or get confused. Often, if someone catches a mistake I'm making, I give them a point,and invite them up to show us their thinking. Occasionally, I'm not wrong, but the student works through a confusion (which others usually share). Similarly, students routinely come up to demonstrate how they got answers. Time permitting, we have people show all the different ways they arrived at the answer. Those who get different answers come up, partly so we can resolve the issue, figure out how and why different answers arose -- which one is \""right,\"" and what error in thinking or calculation caused the mistake. Sometimes students can identify where another student has a confusion before I can, and explain it better, since they have already \""been there,\"" and worked through the error."""	1	0	0	3.5	2	3.5	Education	51f6be9b2fab481200000010	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	5B255AAD05AFDD5C439DBFC6FD1BB65C	7/29/2013 19:12	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	2	None	14

"It's always been a frustration of mine when students focus solely on getting the \right answer\"" and don't realize that being able to explain their thinking or strategy is the key. Students would wait for me to walk them through the steps or copy the answer from a neighbor just to get the answer on the page. I got tired of watching students wait for others around them to do their thinking for them. Recently, I've rearranged my desk groupings and utilized a cooperative group structure where each member of the group is responsible for contributing and being able to explain the thinking involved in solving a problem. As struggles arise, I am available for coaching and they also coach each other. As we share out our answers and strategies, they never know which member of the group will be the \""reporter\"" so they all have to be prepared. This has really helped break that didactic contract. "When Sophie was a camera assistant, she developed her geometric intuition. She figured out the distances and how they changed. An architect develops his geometric intuition, so an artist does. "The teacher first introduced the number talk as a time to think; she also shared with the students the type of problem they would be solving. She unitized the thumbs up tracking system and encouraged those who solved quickly to see the problem in a different way so they remained engaged in the lesson, while learning increased flexibility for problem solving. The teacher continually sought multiple ways of seeing the solution, and modeled the representation of their thinking visually on the board. She encouraged the student who recognized his mistake to share it - talk through it, which he did comfortably; evidently the culture of this classroom highlights mistakes as a welcomed/important part of the learning experience. The teacher also represented on the board in numbers/operations and in pictorial graphs student thinking as the deconstruction of numbers and then again as the flexible rearrangement of them. She asked critical thinking questions of her students, while she showed on the board many ways to think about solving the problem as well as the many solutions that students came up with. Students were asked which property their problem solving strategies and number sentences reflected, given time to talk it over within small groups. "I'd like to push back a little on what you said. I think what the course is trying to show us is that even though students may perform better in the short term when grouped by ability, it has long term negative impacts on their learning. What we need to do is plan classroom activities that allow all students to participate, but by design, the activities let each student take part \at their level\"". For example, in the division problem shown earlier in this session, the teacher didn't group the students by ability. Instead, everyone got the same problem and the same task, \""Make sense of this division problem.\"" They all approached it differently, and even students who were \""advanced\"" and already knew the algorithm were still challenged to understand how other students were solving the problem. That's just one example of differentiation. It takes more planning on the part of the teacher, but once she is experienced with it, it will be much easier and the students will benefit more in the long term."""	1	0	0	4	2.5	3	Education	520d9aefd3941a0e00000014	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	BA2AA11D7D98D05B8C15C27C6812D34A	8/16/2013 3:22	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	520d584921b803160000002f	12

"One thing that has worked in my elementary school is the introduction of daily word problems.  Our administration believes that using math story problems in our classrooms can give every student a chance to develop understanding of basic math concepts.  This has been highly successful.  First, we introduce a real life situation based on our math objective.  We then have the students tell each other the story and what the specific task is.  We then have the students use unifix cubes, drawings, numerical representations of how they solve the problem, using at least one representation that can be put down on paper.  This lets all level of achievers to use whatever forum they want. When higher students finish, we give them the task to solve it another way and show their thinking. As students work individually, the teacher goes around and asks students what they are showing (how they are making sense of their thinking) and selects three students to present their strategies to the class.  These presentations are to be from simple to more complex so that all students can see/relate their thinking to another way of solving the problem.  This has been highly successful in our school practices and has shown us that all students can do math.  I found that at the end of doing this for an entire year, most if not all students were able to express their math thinking with ease and were more than eager to share and be presenters to the class.  I noticed doing daily math word problems also obliterated the anxiety that often accompanies such problems.  Last year, one of my students exclaimed, \I'm not afraid of story problems anymore.\""  This was all the proof I needed.  I'm continuing this practice!"""	1	0	0	6.5	3	3.5	Education	522d63f4c2b1c71600000024	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	46DC28593EF4019E3C5C289AD9BE2BE6	9/9/2013 6:00	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	9

"I teach grade 2 and my students love to use sticky notes. "Why would you not be an advocate for traditional methods? From my science/engineering background, I have an appreciation for techniques that **work**. Traditional techniques work. Newfangled techniques inspired by constructivism, but without the necessary institutional support, don't work.Now, if you had a dispute about what the traditional technique works **for**, then I think that's valid. "I once taught Math SL for the IB program.  Students have the option of taking Math HL (Higher Level), Math SL (Standard Level), or Math Studies.  Students were told which of the classes to take over a 2 year period.  These teacher recommendations were based on grades in Algebra and Geometry. "Almost all assignments or tasks can open up opportunity for differentiated and personalized responses by creatively embedding one or more of these six strategies:1. **Provide guided choices & varied opportunity** (e.g. draw a picture with labels, write an explanation, or create a map to show how how factors or related)2. **Create graphic organizers & relational models** (e.g. create with student input or have student groups represent ideas by using these kinds of graphic representations)3. **Base the task or assignment in a real-world situation and/or within an authentic context** (e.g. as sophisticated as project-based, multi-step challenges and as simple as translating the letters of formulas [abstractions] into the first letter of the things they actually represent [concrete terms])4. **Ask important questions & pose interesting problems** that are meaningful at the students' level (e.g. music-related, sports-related, art-related, car-related, etc.5. **Emphasize clear targets & give honest feedback** (e.g. how close, how far are they in relation to the answer or solution they seek, and what do they need to do next?)6. **Allow assisted learning & technology** (e.g. teaming, cooperative groups, searching on-line, using calculators, etc.)Differentiating the task or assignment help learners gain confidence and competence at their own rate.  The challenge is tracking **responses** vs. tracking students and assignments."	1	0	0	4.5	2.5	3	Education	520d850ed3941a0a00000003	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	5406F5E1E5535F8E2F2E990A84ACC681	8/16/2013 1:49	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	10

"A few years ago, I adopted a system of using three problem sets, based on the ideas at David Suarez's Challenge By Choice blog, http://challengebychoice.wordpress.com/. "The PP students learned how to select and sort information.  They read carefully and decided what previous knowledge was applicable to the new situation. They probably did problems that were multi-step, multi-concept and had little scaffolding. If you want to make small steps in a traditional classroom, here are a few suggestions:1.  Ask the question first. It can be a question you already have, and it does not have to be a great open ended question. Do this right from the beginning of the year so it sets the \tone.\""  You will get complaints at first that you are not \""teaching\"" but the students adjust. Find a problem that has more than one way to do it. Don't show them what to do, just let them work and ask questions.  Hopefully you will get more than one solution to discuss with the class. For example- Give the students 3 ordered pairs and ask if they are all on the same line.  It can be done by graphing, comparing slopes, writing the equation a line through 2 points and showing the third point is on it, or using distances.  If a student finds one method quickly, challenge him to find another. 2.  Don't label or tell the students the \""topic\"" of a problem before you do the problem.  This takes away the necessity of thinking about what skill to use.  AFTER you have finished the problem ask the students how they think the problem should be labeled.  What was the key idea?  What skills did they need?3.  Take the scaffolding out of the problem and let the students figure out what they need to do. Let them decide on their own process. "Cathy set the task then allowed the students to respond. She gave them time- one minute?- to begin their exploration. Two different answers came up. On bringing the class together she asked for an explanation of the two answers. The reasons given were attempts to uncover a rule. At this stage, she stopped them told them that before the end of the class they would have a rule and altered the task to can you make sense of the question/solution. The atmosphere in the class accepted this, there were no visual signs of frustration. Cathy used the language of \yes, but does it make sense?\"" throughout the discussion, never hinting at 'the correctness' of each of the three methods shared. She expected the class to criticise the speaker introducing the roles, asking each to be friendly or sceptical. The 10 minutes were spent reinforcing the mathematical methods of representing problems in different ways, supporting your answers with reasons, analysing other ideas,checking methods through inverse operations; the learning process of re-explaining another point of view and the social learning of collaboration. Only after these processes had been explored was a traditional method introduced."""	1	0	0	4	2.5	2	Education	52087d390757f10e0000002b	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	6E04BA82450553DE0C60CDB32FCA36DE	8/12/2013 6:14	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	13

"I have always been against set grouping of students.  Students change so much as they grow and learn.  They are not all on the same trajectory when they learn, and they may be able to advance quickly in some areas but not in others.  I teach kindergarten, and I pull students to work with me on various tasks in small groups, but the groups are formed based on a particular skill or learning concept and the group members need.  They are not pegged into one group for the whole year.  My groups change as often as the skill or concept has been learned.  Some students exit the group quickly and sometimes others move in.  Many times what many would consider a traditionally high student will be with a traditionally low student because they both need practice with a particular skill or concept.  I don't need to slow down a whole group of students because one needs a lesson, nor do I stop a student from learning something new simply because the others in the group are not ready. "With 8 * 9 * 3, given that student knows the 10-by-10 multiplication table, taking 8 * 9 = 72, and then 70 * 3 + 2 * 3 = 216 (one student), is much more working-memory-efficient than 8 * 3 = 24, and then 24 * 3 * 3, as 24 * 3 is likely to take more working memory in our mind, and similarly for 72 * 3.However, if the student who use the later method can further decompose the problem into 8 * 3 = 24, then 24 * 10 = 240, and then 240 - 24 = 216, it's quite likely that he can get the answer quicker as this is likely to take less working memory."	0	0	1	4	3	3	Education	521cbe4ef25b38120000000e	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	DC9D942E88DE42D1EA594607FCED6A7D	8/27/2013 14:57	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	12

"We do not use ability grouping for math in my school.  Two years ago, in 3rd grade (which is the grade I teach) our administrator asked the 3rd grade team to split our students by ability for reading.  We did this for several reasons, but primarily because we had to document for RTI (Response to Intervention) for those students reading below grade level.  We used several tools to determine where to place children and the children were never told that they were being \grouped\"", just that we were changing teachers for reading groups. [And, yes, some of them could figure out what we were doing.]  The groups were fluid, however, so that if a child made significant progress in reading ability, he or she was \""moved\"" to another teacher (essentially another/higher group).  What we discovered was that those children who were so very low that they couldn't read was that once they were placed in a very small class, they began to participate more AND their reading difficulties became more obvious.  Why? Because suddenly those children could not disappear into the larger group.  They felt more at ease responding because they were in the same boat as everyone else at the reading table.  Most of those children made huge strides in their reading levels.As a teacher I noticed that even though we used several tools, some children were incorrectly placed.  The students in my class were reading way beyond the 3rd grade level and were considered the advanced group; however, some of those students simply did not have the maturity to be in such a class and found themselves way over their heads.I know this is not about math and I recognize the problems with grouping or labeling; however, I see the benefits for those 3rd graders who are so woefully behind in their reading skills.  They need that small group setting--those intervention strategies to bring them up to speed."""	0	0	0	4	3	3	Education	51ed8769b81a820a00000082	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	ED6EF73DB867E68709DDE4C81D313970	7/22/2013 19:26	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51ed7e36b81a82160000007c	38

"Your first equation is a good representation of the problem.  The goal now is to find out what 'x' is.  Your second equation doesn't get you any closer to that goal, nor the third.  In such a problem I tell students that we are trying to find out what x is, not what 4x is, or x + 2, but just x.  To do that we need some kind of an answer such as \x = .....\"".  To get there we need to get x all by itself by using manipulations that maintain the sanctity of the equals sign.  This is where the creativity comes in -- the student can do whatever they want.  Some manipulations will get closer to the goal of \""x - ....\"", some won't.  It doesn't matter how fast they get there.  Doing manipulations that don't help helps the student see what will and what won't help.  You could view this as making a mistake if the goal is to get to \""x = ...\"" as quickly as possible.  This is where the learning comes in.  From your first equation, if the student was stuck, I'd point out there are an awful lot of x's there, is there a way to put them together."""	1	0	1	4	3	2.5	Education	520a70cb84e4c6160000005e	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	9EF412184C1E2F2AF8939916811554BE	8/13/2013 17:45	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	5207b9d5508b3c1200000012	51

"When students are taught procedures before they are given a chance to explore a concept, they are, by necessity, limited in their ability to think mathematically. The simplicity of the question provides every student with an entry point to the question. "Hi Margherite,From a maths tutors point of view (and student teacher), all I can suggest is to ask students more questions which require them to explain their steps and how and why the standard algorithm works. "I have tried all different types of grouping, and my favorite way is what I call A/B partners.  I change up these partners throughout the year - sometimes they are based on confidence, sometimes on types of thinkers (pictorial vs. abstract), sometimes it is just random.  I have tables in my room, so I have 3 sets of a/b partners at each table unless someone is absent of I have an odd numbered group, then there are 2 As and a B, or visa-versa.  With A/B partners I have the As explain something to the Bs, or the B's, to the As, and then often times the table group will then discuss as a group comparing their solutions and discussing things.  I've found that by having flexible groups, students don't feel like they are being pigeon holed into a particular group.  I've also found that sometimes students surprise me because they may work really well with a particular partner and they both really bring out the best thinking in one another.  Also, it allows students to work with different types of personalities, which is also a good life skill.  Therefore, I think grouping should be flexible and change often."	1	0	0	4	3.5	2	Education	520ed65ed59d510e0000005c	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	BEA3DB64E6EF65A903AA3711E79E701D	8/17/2013 1:48	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	12

"I am on the fence re the argument against grouping/laning, whatever you want to call it.As an example, one year at our elementary school, our 3rd graders were chosen to pilot a district math program. "It's easier to grasp if you begin with simple numbers. For example, If I start with a piece of wood that is 12 inches long, how many 2-inch pieces can I get out of it? Answer: 6 pieces of wood, each 2-inches long. That's the same as 1 divided by 1/6.    If I start with a piece of wood that is 12 inches long, how many 3-inch pieces can I get? Answer: 4 pieces. That's 1 divided by 1/4.    If I start with a piece of wood that is 12 inches long, how many 6-inch pieces can I get? Answer: 2 pieces. That's 1 divided by 1/2.  So far, all these lengths (2,3,6) are factors of 12, so we get whole number answers. The number of pieces we get goes down as the length of the piece desired increases.   If I start with a piece of wood that is 12 inches long, how many 8-inch pieces can I get? Answer: 1 piece that is 8-inches plus one piece leftover that is 4 inches (half the desired length), or 1.5 8-inch pieces.  That's 1 divided by 2/3."	1	0	1	4	2	3	Education	52069bd09df35b9b0400004b	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	E9F462AE642C321536A5643D9CEAD76D	8/10/2013 20:00	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51fdde602c9f280e0000003d	188

"I currently thank students for making mistakes, and explain them to the class saying it's important to see what works, and where it's easy to go wrong. "Not an easy solution, but one possible approach is to have students working in mixed ability groups within the classroom.  Then, with enough structure and practice, students learn that full discussions within their groups where they are helping each other must come before asking a teacher for help.  Although sometimes there still are a few students who continue to struggle or disengage and it becomes frustrating to the highest achievers, usually the strong students find that explaining and teaching helps them to solidify and better understand their own learning.  In addition, having challenge problems or extensions for almost every activity/problem/assignment encourages the strongest students to take their thinking further.  Ideally, students themselves generate the \next question\"" or engage enough in the material to want to pose a further problem.  I recognize that all this sounds almost impossible, but with good grouping I've seen it work. "I teach adult students and it's not uncommon to hear \I can't do math\"" or \""I hate math\"". "Much of stereotyping is pre-conscious (or unconscious).  We make judgements before we know that we have.  Before we \think.\""  The judgements come out in gestures, inflections, subtle expressions that we are not even aware of.  It could be the student that we call on, the smile that we give.  If we are to counter these things of which we are not conscious in our interactions with others we must do so consciously and conscientiously.  We have to make a point to compensate.For me I find this easier to do with young kids than with adults sometimes.  When it is a parent about my age that I am working with I feel that I more easily slip.  thoughts will pop into my head and I will think, \""where did that come from?\""  Or with  young adults I often do the same.  Quick judgements can be very accurate, but we need to also question them reflectively and ensure that we are not perpetuating negative typing.We will never completely get rid of stereotypes.  Our mind sorts automatically to create quick judgements of people.  It is how we have evolved.  However, we know that many of these can be negative (and completely inaccurate), and as educators we need to confront these in ourselves (even if we would like to deny that they exist) and ensure that we treat each student with dignity."""	1	0	0	4.5	4	2	Education	51e770b2a5474f160000011c	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	9ADCD39A9B3A06838F850BEEA7B63C7B	7/18/2013 4:36	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	2	None	10

"There are three things I would like to discuss. One is the power of having different sets of numbers that push on the same ideas that you want students to explore. So for example, if you are a second grade teacher and you are helping students think about subtraction, or difference, you might ask children to consider the same situation but with different numbers: for example, in one class students were asked to measure two different objects, determine which was longer, and then to figure out how much longer the longer object was than the shorter.Children chose the objects to measure, but the teacher was able to support students who were struggling by asking them to first find the difference between two objects close in size. On the other hand, those who quickly found the difference in length between two items were challenged to find the difference between two objects which varied greatly in length.In the end, the teacher had the whole class work together in groups to determine the way in which the difference in length between two objects she held in her hands could be determined. This was connected with the position of the numbers on the number line.So, the numbers and situations were different and appropriate for different students, but the conversation around the meaning of difference, its relationship to the relative position of numbers on the number line,  and how to determine what the difference is,  was held with everyone.In another class, the teacher routinely posted different sets of numbers for problem solving and students chose those which were an appropriate challenge for them.The second thing I want to discuss is my opposition to pairing children who are at very different places in their mathematical understanding. "I have taught mixed level math classes for several years, but found that there were always several at the low end who found it difficult to keep up with the rest of the class and several at the top end who \got\"" the concepts faster than everyone else. "One thing I've read about is that Support classes find unusual success when they pre-teach the material, rather than re-teach the material already covered. Think about it this way, when you use Support primarily to re-teach, you're admitting to the students that they're slower, that they're not as smart. Many of them are willing to take the Support Class because they want the extra assistance, but it is a subtle acknowledgement that they aren't \smart.\"" When you pre-teach the material, you're decreasing the cognitive load that the students will go through on the day of class. Instead of \""Factoring?!? What does that word mean?\"", they've practiced the word in resource class, and perhaps did some 4th-grade multiplication/factorization review and started the basics. Now, when they're in a group with high and low kids, the kids from the Support class have background knowledge to contribute. They're smart! They also will be able to follow along better with the lectured that's designed for-the-middle, because the very basics were covered the day before in Support class. And, the kids who traditionally get rewarded for having the background knowledge (the hand-raising volunteer types) have to step up their game because they suddenly have a lot more competition for teacher's pet. I don't remember what study it was that showed this effect, but it's definitely something to look into. It makes much better use of time than having a kid sit lost and confused through the difficult material, and then handing them easier work the next day in Support class. It sends mixed messages as to what rigor level is expected, and it can mean that the main math class was a waste because the kid didn't feel comfortable with the word Factorization and thus 90 minutes of material went over his head. I also have seen the Support classes can turn into hand-holding classes where the steps are more and more broken down by the teacher who is \""assisting\"" the student, whereas when the material is being pre-taught, the goal of the Support class is about growing your background knowledge on a topic up to a comfortable level, and it's becomes a safe place for asking questions you don't know, which will be helpful when you learn them \""for real\"" tomorrow. Anyway, best of luck - hope this helped!"""	1	0	0	4	2.5	3	Education	51f8de4e775ca41600000007	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	9A9CB58419A0E6FB4B138E1AD75398F8	7/31/2013 9:52	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51f88e2399a7c60a0000009f	6

"The principle reason for these negative messages is that Math actually is hard. It is one of those areas where students have to put in true pencil effort to learn. It is never enough to simply go to class and listen. The brain that flourishes in a course like Literature or History is used to remembering everything it hears and processing it immediately. With a well-developed auditory memory, this type of learning occurs without the student's awareness. While reading is necessary (although I remember attending a Masters seminar on Proust in which one of my classmates delighted in making contributions that superficially appeared to be based on his perusal of the material when in fact he rarely kept up with the assigned reading) most readers do not think of reading as an effort. But math requires actual effort. If at first you do not succeed, you must try again, rewrite the problem, learn to sleep on it, learn to push yourself to do what you do not find easy. Math is the vegetable portion of school offerings. It is good for you but you must 'develop a taste for it.'Naturally, many adults  including parents and even educators persist in propagating a set of negative messages. "I don't work in a classroom - I tutor homeschooled and special needs students who need a different way of teaching for each one.  I can imagine it is hard to try to accommodate everyone's needs but I do think it can be done. I helped in the classroom and saw how the center offered a chance for each student to work at their own level on same or similar tasks.  In response to a prompt that often was built around the monthly theme of homes or gardens or the circus, etc., one student might have been using base 10 blocks to model a problem with adding tens and ones, while another used pencil and paper to add and carry 3-4 places, or another drew images showing addition, and so on. A parent helper or aide would be there to offer support and inspiration. Or sometimes it was set up so that one station had similar but more complicated tasks, the next had easier concepts or tasks, and the third, a simpler task yet, and the student could choose the task that was at their level. "I tell students, honestly, when I'm told that it is my job to do their work that no, I wrote my own job description, and no where does it say I'm supposed to do John's work. I then add that I've taught math longer than he has, and I add that I don't have the problem here -- he does. I make sure to always give students the choice to grow or quit. Kids want power struggles, and I tell them when they are ready, I will be there.My rules are simple:1. A student must always come up with an answer first, and they must memorize the gist of the problem. I pick up their paper and have them prove this. I tell them I expect mistakes and frustration and for them to feel dumb and unsure; if I didn't want this, I'd assign these middle schoolers connect the dots and 1+1 problems. Of course, no one would learn anything.2. The work must be in writing. Then I make students defend what they've done. Why? Many students flat out lie. Very brazen, but so many people artificially inflate students' self-esteem that they don't know how to deal with disappointment (I have a growth mindset, but yes, I'm disappointed in failure; I bet Edison was disappointed 8,999 times until he got the light bulb correct, and imagine how different it would be today if he had stumbled on the correct method the first time!).3. "There were several strategies that Cathy used.  She encouraged every group to come up with an opinion.  She introduced the topic first and then the algorithm, focusing rather on students making sense of the problem.  She had students talking and working together in groups. "One idea that I tried to show students what persistence looked like was to take a problem and work through it myself using a document camera at the front of the room.  My goal was not to solve the problem, but to show the kids how I approached the problem, what I was thinking as I solved the problem, everything that I said to myself as I solved it, trying different ways to solve it, and going back to check my thinking. "Four years ago, my first year teaching, I was warned about a \difficult\"" student before the start of the school year. I was told to put his mother's phone number on my cell so I could call her immediately when he gave me trouble. No one had anything positive to say about him. I was troubled by the universally negative view of this child and was determined to give him a positive experience in a classroom. During the first week I called his mom. She picked up the phone and said, \""What has he done now?\"" I told her how nice it was to have him in my class (I had made sure to make the call during the \""honeymoon\"" period) and I gave specific examples of things he had done successfully in class and mentioned that I saw that he clearly had the potential to do well. I heard a huge sigh of relief. We talked about working together to make this year a good stepping off point for high school and that I wanted to try to channel his energy into being a leader. Throughout the year, I continued to reinforce my belief in his potential by identifying examples of clear mathematical thinking even when he might have made arithmetic errors. His mom and I spoke frequently and only one of those conversations had to be about \""problem\"" behavior. This experience was not universal among his other teachers.I guess this is a kind of long winded way of giving an example of the positive impact of demonstrating true belief in a student's potential by looking past the \""bad kid\"" stereotype with which he had always lived."""	1	0	0	6	2	3	Education	51eaf4d61702790e0000005f	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	C1059ECAF79F2891D21E59B16ED2E85F	7/20/2013 20:36	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	1	None	69

"I can relate to the research on this issue of grouping. I am not a teacher, but I can definitely see these ideas in play when I was a student and now as my six year old son is going through school. "I really liked Vivian's approach as it was closest to mine.  Having spent an inordinate amount of time in arcades as a young child, I learned that 4 quarters makes a dollar very quickly.  So, when I saw this problem, I immediately took 29/4 and got 7 remainder 1, which means 700 with 1 quarter left over...725.  This process has similarities to i^29  = i and other situations where certain groupings reproduce patterns.  Another example is \what is the last digit of 9^1000?\""  This problem produces an overflow error on most calculating devices, but we can solve by looking for a pattern within the last digit and then dividing the 1000 by the number of numbers in our pattern and applying the remainder.  So, what I'm trying to say here is that I thought that putting Vivian's method in the category of the distributive property was nice, but the distributive property may not have been what she was really thinking.  She may have simply been grouping 4 quarters to make dollars.  While interpreting this in light of the distributive property is excellent, is it not also excellent to think of grouping the 29 into groups of 4 to make 100's with either 0, 25, 50, or 75 left over?  If we happened to be in the context of counting quarters, I would suggest that this is what we would have done...make stacks of 4 quarters until we used our quarters up then count the hundreds and than count the leftovers by 25 cents apiece."""	1	0	0	4.5	3	3	Education	51f7b18199a7c60e00000015	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	A1E8F07C46885A676126BCCA568F0B40	7/30/2013 12:28	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	30

"When talking about mistakes being helpful for brain growth, there was little attention on what happens in the case of recalling information (and providing a correct answer) without making a mistake. It was almost implicit that what happened was \no growth\"".I have a theory based on what I learned about neural networks. When training a  neural network, there are 2 activities, creating new connections and reinforcing \""good\"" existing connections. This reinforcement was critical for producing a well trained network and it was what made occasional \""bad\"" connections unimportant. Recall activity, if not conducive to growth, it may play a key role in this reinforcement portion and still be extremely important.Neural network learning curves are often modeled using a sigmoid function (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigmoid_function), this describes the fact that initial learning is shallow, but after some reinforcement it gets to a point where the learning becomes much stronger very quickly (where the slope of the sigmoid becomes much steeper) and then it reaches saturation, where it takes a lot more effort to produce an improvement. The key may be in finding the right balance between growth and reinforcement. If we focus too much on reinforcement (which may be a problem in the current education systems) then we reach saturation point and simply get diminishing returns. When we're close to saturation, focusing on growth is likely to produce much better results, but I believe there is also risk if focusing too much on the growth mindset and not providing sufficient reinforcement.Of <nameRedac_<anon_screen_name_redacted>> this is very speculative, and based on extrapolation from research done for other purposes that may or may not apply here. "I would be happy to comment on the subject of learning from our mistakes. There are different kinds of mistakes: I made a simple error that I must go back and find, e.g., a calculation was done incorrectly or I misapplied a procedure or concept; or, worse, I am completely operating in the dark and am grasping at straws and cannot navigate my way through the forest. When students make the first type of mistake, they can learn how to correct their conceptual or procedural bearings, or correct the simple mis-calculation.  But, when the student has no idea conceptually of what the problem entails, they will have greater difficulty learning from the mistake if the concept, procedure, or calculation does not become clear in the process of revising.How does this make all of us feel?When I was taking classes in higher math in the ™old days,š I learned the procedure from the professor and knew how to identify a procedure with an exercise or a problemand there is a difference between the two. "In working with students on such problems I abandon the goal of representing the situation in one variable and let them use A, B, and C to start with. I don't see a need to use just one variable, and having 3 variables allows the students to keep the original problem in their head a little longer in working the problem. Jumping right to using 'x' to show the relationship between the three piles is too big a step.  So:  B = A + 2; C = 4A; A + B + C = 14.  Then I talk about the importance of the equals sign.  The equals sign is a like a balance scale.  The equals sign means you have the same amount of stuff on the left that you do on the right.  The equals sign means that the thing on the left (same amount of stuff as the right) can be substituted for the thing on the right anywhere it appears in this problem.  And vise versa -- the thing on the right can be substituted for the thing on the left anywhere it appears in the problem.  So in this case, you can substitute A + 2 for B anywhere it appears in this situation, and 4A for C anywhere it appears in this situation.  So A + B + C = 14 can become A + (A + 2) + (4A) = 14.  I will actually write out A + B + C = 14 with lots of space, and then erase the B and write \(A + 2)\"" in its place; erase C and write \""(4A)\"" in its place.  At this point I will point out we now have a mathematical representation of the problem of piles of rocks and how many is in each pile.  We check that this mathematical representation truly does represent the problem.  Then I ask them for a leap of faith -- to not think about the original problem, but just look at the equation.  Now there is one variable in the equation and let's find out what it is -- view it as a puzzle.  I let them do any manipulation they want to as long as that manipulation honors the equals sign.  We look at the result of each manipulation, asking does it make the equation look less complex -- always keeping in mind that at this point, the goal is to get to \""A = ...\"" -- finding out what A is.  Once we have A, I have the student look back at the original problem and tell me what we've found out.  I ask have we answered the question originally asked?  If a single variable, such as x is used, it is easy to think the problem is solved once we find x.  But by using A, and looking back at the original problem, we find that we know A, but there is still more work to do to find B and C."""	1	0	0	4	2	3	Education	520a730ad227f90a00000016	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	9EF412184C1E2F2AF8939916811554BE	8/13/2013 17:55	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	49

"Reading through some of these responses caused me to contemplate what I saw as the 'gap' between parents and children - by this I mean, what happened to create the type of parent that essentially fears maths and is then forced to feel this fear again when talking to the teachers of their children or when faced with being asked for help with maths homework by their offspring.I then thought about my Y11 class from last year. "Something that might be done after students have been working together in a group for a few weeks.  I would assume that as a teacher I have been providing instruction about how to work together effectively in groups, with students assigned roles and given tasks that are worthy of a group effort. Students would have had the opportunity to take up different roles within the group, and explicit attention would have been paid to issues surrounding status and the importance of valuing everyone's voice.I would then give students a sheet with the outline of a large hand drawn on it.  Students would write their name on the paper and pass it to the student on their right in the group.  Everyone then would be asked to write down one attribute that they felt the student whose paper they had, had brought to the group to help it function more effectively.  The paper could then be passed on around the group so that everyone in the group had the opportunity to provide feedback to the group member.As a teacher I would collect these, at least the first time I did something like this, to check that the comments were appropriate. "This activity is more of an attempt to raise self-awareness for the instructor, but could be extended to include students. Prior to mathematics class, put two empty cans or jars bearing the labels male and female somewhere in the classroom where they are easy to access. Have a bag of beans, paper clips, pennies, or other small objects near the jars. During class, each time you interact with a student place a bean in the appropriate jar according to the gender of the student(s) with whom you were interacting. Which gender gets the most interaction? How could you further stratify the data? How about paying attention to the length of interactions, the topic of interaction, and/or the tone of interaction. "Even in \tracked groups\"" there is no \""average\"" or \""typical.\""   All learners have very different needs and approaches.  I prefer differentiation and propose that well-developed options, all aimed at the same or similar learning goals, empowers students to learn the same things in different ways.  It also leads to far more interesting responses for assessment.   The challenge for the teacher is in coming up with substantive options that allow for different forms of expression while expecting learners to concentrate on the same learning goals. There is an art to differentiation, and it is an area for skill development and practice for every teacher. There are many ways to differentiate instruction and/or assignments.  My favorites are choices of: (a) visual & logical models, (b) questions & problems, (c) real-world & authentic contexts, (d) clear targets & honest feedback, (e) assisted learning/teams & technology."""	1	0	0	4.5	3.5	2	Education	5227b80b9880f80a00000009	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	5406F5E1E5535F8E2F2E990A84ACC681	9/4/2013 22:45	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	11

"I have a very interesting format that I use for my students interactive math journals. I give them the notes - starting with their goal at the top. "I am not sure whether any setting can be justified, however there is a great deal of mileage in enabling students to aspire. As a head of mathematics at a secondary school in the UK I have often been asked how can we ensure we are adding value to each and every child, thereby enabling each child to fulfil their potential and grow as students of mathematics. I agree with many of Jo Boaler's sentiments especially giving students implicit fixed mindset messages regarding setting arrangements in schools, which has given me much food for thought. Setting does pose a number of issues, none more so than students being pigeonholed into a stereotype, as attainment within set 1 within one struggling school could be working at the same standard as a student within set 4 of a geographically and socio-economically different school considered outstanding. That said as a school that does set its students there are a range of supporting mechanisms that I think we use well, which can help alleviate some of the fixed mindset messages she talks about. One of the main ones involves team teaching opportunities which involves teaming up students within various groups to complete tasks, equally setting tasks across year groups and encouraging students to complete assignments collaboratively, with another students from another group. Equally i feel strongly that students can achieve a sense of achievement in the maths classroom by drawing on a variety of creative strands. Using cross curricular strands which celebrate other aspects of school life, and particular strengths of the students. These opportunities may draw upon skills that students may consider to be outside the normal parameters of the mathematics classroom. Also much of mathematical attainment is closely allied to motivation to learn. Some of those motivations can be intrinsic in nature. However it is my experience that students view a mathematics qualification as desirable as it enables them to access other qualifications and career paths. Mathematics therefore as a gatekeeper qualification is one of the necessary career related and dependent qualifications, therefore there can be some mileage in informing students of opportunities open to them and using that as a driver for performance, therefore taking away issues and comparisons with peer attainment."	1	0	0	4.5	3.5	2.5	Education	51f906ec775ca41600000010	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	A67302413D0CFD14CE3C3D456B427C09	7/31/2013 12:45	CommentThread	TRUE	FALSE	0	None	18

"I teach at a private school and we have always had tracking in the middle school and high school levels. Until this past year, we also had tracking at the elementary level. "I teach high school chemistry and I have two levels of groups: a regular level and honors level. My observations are of two sides: 1. I cannot imagine these two levels mixed! My high achievers would be bored to death and will just not show up. My lower level students will get lost, will shut out, and will not show up either. I believe that, at least in high school, division into ACHIEVEMENT levels (not ABILITY levels!) is very important. It provides an opportunity for better prepared students to stay interested and engaged, and learn more. It also affords students less prepared more time to work on the concepts and, again, learn more.2. On another hand, the division is far from perfect and each of these groups contains mixed levels. There are students placed in the wrong level, either higher or lower than fits their readiness level. In all cases it would be a disaster to ignore the obvious disconnect. I think that ANY two students are on two levels and require differentiated approach. It is up to the teacher to recognize \misplaced\"" students and prepare materials on a few levels inside each grouping. It is very hard to do, no doubts. With our already super-busy overload, it is hard to find the time and energy to prepare multilevel lessons, however it is critical for student learning. In addition to that, we all stay after school to help those who still need more time and more training.So the bottom line: achievement grouping is needed (at least in high school math and sciences), but it does not replace a teacher who teaches all learners on many levels."""	1	0	0	3.5	4	2	Education	51f93aab2b8ed91600000098	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	88C6FE1D709F036498CEB682D1101F29	7/31/2013 16:26	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	8

"Students form their identity around the courses they take.  They have a math identity.  By tracking or putting them in groups by ability, we are preassigning that identity for them and for everyone else.  Student's assigned to certain \level\"" of classes(low, medium, high, honors,etc) now have this image of themselves as that descriptor.  Once student's are put in those classes and are tracked (which happens at an early age), parents, teachers and society buy in to said descriptor.  Oh Tommy, he is ok at math but not great because he is the middle class. Or Jenny is great at math she is in honors.  There is a lot of pressure and identity assigned along the continuum that supports a fixed mindset.  Jenny is less likely to take risks in math lest she loose her standing.  Upward or downward mobility is limited and those on the bottom will likely remain there through high school and those on top fear of losing this position.  Mathematical achievement of the individual begins to ossify with this identity or class level.  Students on the \""lower\"" end will achieve to the standard that has been assigned and no more.  While students at the \""higher\"" end will also be cautious in achievement because they have been held to a higher standard of \""smart\"" and do not want to loose it."""	1	0	0	3.5	4	2	Education	52025521b65d7d120000007b	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	B70D792764DDC17FEC9733EA5813E567	8/7/2013 14:09	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	2	None	46

"This past school year, I taught a Grade 9/10 split locally developed math course. It is the lowest level tracked math class. "Openness - By phrasing the question \how do you see the shapes growing\"" as your first question, it opened the discussion up to all students. Avoiding this question in version 2 lacks that openness and buy in for the students. Not everyone could answer the final question right away and may give up quickly, but your initial question gets the buy in for the follow up question.The initial question also showed that there are different ways of seeing the pattern, and is a great point for discussion and comparison with other students. In version 2, the question may be too directed to allow a variety of ways to see it.The different ways of seeing, allow different entry points to solving the problem, different paths and strategies can be used. Another option that wasn't shown (to arrive at the answer) was to rearrange the stacks by taking the furthest one right and placing it on the the one left of middle. Then take the \""two-stack\"" and place on the one two-left of middle. Then take the \""three-stack\"" and place on the one three-left of middle. This pattern always generates a square, and we can now see the reason (n+1)^2 is the answer.Both versions of the task had a goal, but the first version allowed immediate peer feedback by comparing the visualization right away. "Mistakes are so important in YOUR development,GRADES will partially be based on the number of mistakes made toward success. Here is how it works, on the Friday quiz there will be 10 problems to take home over the weekend. "Many students view their education as a series of tasks to be completed, rather than a means of preparation for the tasks of adulthood; they quantify the point of termination rather than grasping the concept of lifelong learning. Thus, this mindset lowers the priority given education. They see lessons and courses as things to be completed; skills learned are not put fully to use because there is minimal pressure to do so. An analogy is learning to drive: You study a book of rules and regulations to pass a test for a learners permit, which is used to actually practice operating the vehicle. You then demonstrate highway and parking skills and are awarded a license. At that point, a marginal (knowledgable, yet unexperienced and potentially dangerous) driver joins all others. It is continued practice, full of trial and errors, that makes this person a more competent driver ... until old age begins reversing the process. The incentives for improvement driving skills are the likelihood of killing oneself or others, loss of driving privileges due accidents, and expense of vehicle repairs and medical costs. Math, like driving, is a series of skills that must be used (applied) in order to be retained, used successfully and improved."	1	0	0	4	4	2	Education	51e858cf73317f0a000000a6	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	B8CC3F1D0D53D2EC22A541BE70D59456	7/18/2013 21:06	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	9

"We have some very high-powered math learners whose parents demand courses that push them. One thing I'm not seeing discussed here is learning style. "My understanding of differentiated instruction is that the concept that there is one concept being taught to the class but the work that students do, will most likely be different. The teacher may discreetly give different work to students, or students may get to choose the work that they want to complete. For example, say the students are working on problem solving and they are given a question about a dragon dance. The students might be allowed to choose different ways to solve the problem - drawing, plasticine etc or maybe the teacher will change the numbers in the problem for students to create a more challenging exercise. The teacher may work with different little groups as needed, but it's never the same people in the same groups all the time. "I think that grouping or \streaming\"" as we call it here in India is a particularly sad practice as it's founded on a false premise. Prof. Kurt Fischer's research at HGSE has shown that learning development is not linear but proceeds in a sort of upward trending saw tooth type waveform. This means that you could get wildly different results of children's ability depending on how well their learning development is \""in phase\"", as it were.My small research group uses proprietary wireless keyboards to allow each child to answer each question in parallel. We provide representations of class responses immediately after the responses have come in. We subsequently analyse how student performance can be improved through studying the archives of student responses.We believe this motivates each child because each child is responded to. Additionally, children retain their own privacy as we do not identify individual responses in the representations. I think that we fundamentally share a strong belief that performance is a function of effort and persistence, and somehow the children pick up on this thinking.We also found almost zero instances of indiscipline in a 30 hour study. Finally we found that our maths curriculum which is almost totally at variance with the school curriculum resulted in the experimental group registering significant improvement over the control group even in end of term tests run by the school. The average change in performance based on US developed placement tests went from <25% to >75%.We have videos of the classes and the report of the study is available at www.agem.in/pdf/BriefReport.pdf"""	1	0	0	5	2.5	3	Education	51fc01340d1d360e00000040	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	586FF5481D6B36E5535F27A82C4F4046	8/2/2013 18:57	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	1	51eedf9e4620910a00000051	65

"In the past I have used \fuzzies\"" (fuzzy shaped drawings on the board, numbered 1-5, with 1 having a big happy face and music playing around it, to 3 having a straight mouth and being very neutral, to 5 having a very angry face and steam rising from it).  Students draw the fuzzy and number that best represents how they feel about math. We then share as a group.  We show the pictures to each other and talk about why we feel the way we do. With all the new research and awareness of how this in not most beneficial to learners we need to shift our thinking and utilize students' strengths to the benefit of all who are in a class.  One of the best examples of this I find is when students peer teach.  They can talk out their understanding and ideas while at the same time seeing another persons perspective.  One of the comments that resonated with me was when Jo talked about teaching to the middle of the pack and not challenging students enough.  I feel very strongly that all students need to feel challenged and that even those who might require additional support when learning something new should still be challenged to engage in the more difficult problems.  We as teachers can easily adjust the volume f work that is assigned to students, but we should not sacrifice the complexity of the material believing that our students are not capable of handling it.  I teach at a school where the majority of our students have diagnosed LD (approx 75%) and the remainder have either undiagnosed challenges learning in a typical school environment or have had very negative past experiences and wish to learn with a more structured and supportive environment.  We have often grouped our classes on perceived ability.  We are starting to move away from this classification in the hopes that we can still provide the necessary support for each student but also expose each of them to challenging material.  As I mentioned above, I believe that past grouping was done with their success put first, but perhaps not in recognizing that this was not the case.  I am looking forward to seeing how a more heterogenous group will perform and I am excited to see some of my students who have not had success in the past work through challenging material and succeed."	1	0	0	5	2.5	3	Education	521a6c3bc838ab160000001c	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	7A5E723E64E8AF1DA0291F3B07BF57E5	8/25/2013 20:42	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51e7f4ea73317f160000001d	421

"I liked the way Kathy kept the conversation rolling. "The conversations with Chris and Sebastian resonated the most with me. The messages I received from them are that students intuitively understand mathematics but we \mess it up\"" with abstractions. Students need to learn how to apply and generalize what they intuitively know is true. Chris said that students need to develop the self-confidence to know that if they think, research and collaborate, they can solve problems they have never seen before. Sebastian said that students make the mistake of trying to use formulae and facts that they don't really understand. Both implied that it is necessary to allow students TIME to understand concepts and make connections. At this point it struck me that this is not just about lessons. "I am a teacher of high school music and we labour severely under the popular perception that music is a 'gift' or a 'talent' - that somehow you either are musical or you are not. Thankfully, the flipside of the disinterest my administrators feel in my subject means that I have a huge amount of freedom in regard to pedagogy and curriculum. One of the most successful changes I have implemented as the Head of Department is in the area of assessment. Instead of formal tests or exams each student fills in a profile sheet at the beginning of each term. The sheet asks them to specify six goals (one each in six areas of skill) from a selection which spans a large range of proficiencies (from beginner/primary to tertiary level).  Students self-assess where they want to work on this sliding scale and what they believe they want to/need to achieve in order to progress. We discuss this in groups (and individually if necessary) but I will never change a student's selection.  They then have all term to demonstrate their six skills to the class and themselves at any time they choose. They can have as many attempts at demonstrating the skill as they like, every week if they choose or only once a term if they choose. Once they have demonstrated understanding by applying it successfully to a problem (not one posed by me but one that they or their peers came up with), I sign their profile sheet and congratulate them. "Dot card number talks could also help students to see and understand logic how associative and distributive laws work separately and how they work together [two groups of (3 + 2) = two groups of three + two groups of two]. In the essence we are breaking composite numbers into meaningful chunks and re-grouping them: horizontal grouping [(3 + 2) + (3 + 2)], vertical grouping (2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2), diagonal grouping (2 + 4 + 3 + 1), grouping equal chunks in each second row [(3 + 3) + (2 + 2)] and then adding different groups.We can use dot cards even for imagining a bigger (non-existing) chunk and subtracting from it a missing difference (by using extra dots of different color).This particular (or similar) pattern can be used for discussing not only addition and multiplication but division as well: we can break 10 into 2 groups of five (horizontal grouping of factors) or five groups of two (vertical grouping of factors)."	1	0	0	4	2.5	3	Education	52206f368b435d160000002b	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	C4CA4AC115314C138EA4CE81B158E6DF	8/30/2013 10:08	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	11

"I agree that is important to stress the concept of symmetry and balance with the equals sign. Sometimes to illustrate the point, I have  two students come to the front of the room and I give them trays that they hold in front of themselves. Then I put objects on the trays and ask the students to act as if they were a pan balance scale. The object of the game is for the students w the trays to stay in balance while other student pile objects of \known weights\"" on the scale. The class gives them instructions as to what to put on the scale and what to take off the scale, so that they can remain in balance. Then we try to represent this situation symbolically by drawing the scale and objects, and then with equations. It's a fun diversion and it helps them to make a connection between the equation on the paper and the idea of balance. "As many have noted, all of these seem to play into one-another. If we work backward from where the problem exists, perhaps there are issues around *how* material is presented at the college level. This can be compared to how it is presented at the 7-12 level, often reflected in procedures/formula-focused-content-specific \drive\"" to complete chapters. The material is presented from the math-expert's (teacher) standpoint, the single-subject teacher; whereas, at an elementary level the material is (hopefully) presented from a teaching standpoint, the multiple-subject teacher with methods courses behind him/her to support teaching/learning for all. At the next level, again moving backwards, it is possible that Algebra continues to be the \""gate-keeper,\"" as our math department chair calls it. If students are successful in Algebra, the doors open to other mathematics. It is essential that students *understand* the material of course, so simply earning an A in Algebra is not equivalent to long-term understanding or conceptual synthesis. Moving along, it is also possible that students simply do not have the foundational knowledge necessary for success - which loops all of these together. How are we teaching elementary students? Are we teaching for understanding? Are we assessing FOR learning rather than as a measure to check the end of the chapter in a book? Are we using multiple approaches and are we considering multiple procedures for finding an answer? Is the \""right\"" answer (the algorithm) always the answer itself? Do we discuss math and make it part of common classroom culture (much like the literacy corner or Word Wall)? The list goes on... but leads back to the foundational understanding which links to the last thought: students believe they don't have the ability. I will end by saying math came easy to me, I breezed through math in ES and MS, it became a bit more challenging in HS but I relied on my ability to memorize and use formulas in MS to make the most of HS math. College courses in undergrad were mostly GE requirements, and later methods courses for my teaching credential; however, it wasn't until I was *teaching* math that I finally UNDERSTOOD what the underlying mathematics were. "In my school in Ontario, Canada we do the group work in the context of a three-part lesson (see work of Marian Small).  The group work is done after the first part of the lesson which activates knowledge the children already have.  For example, if I wish the children to use groups to count (Grade 1), then the intro will have them practicing skip counting by 5 or 2's etc.  Then they work in arbitrary groups which change every day.  I wish them to be exposed to many different methods of thinking.  We call this a three part lesson (the third part being a whole group review of the work of the students where they comment on the math).  I am sure others are using it.  At first everyone wants to work with the 'smart' person in the class, but over the course of the year that changes.  I had never thought about it before, but I think this goes a long way toward dispelling the myth that only some can learn math.  The students see that even the students who may struggle can come up with great strategies to overcome their own struggles and this inspires others to do the same."	1	0	0	5	3	3	Education	52052107d01fec160000006e	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	DB3D34C6DE6508706CCC4BC8F93E7ADC	8/9/2013 17:04	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51eeeff9462091120000005d	55

"I would agree with you Jim. My school has recently implemented tracking for year 7 (the lowest year level) as a means to lift the abysmal test results that students have been getting. However the ability grouping has been narrowly defined (by test scores and teacher judgements in one area of maths) and what we have found is that there is still wide variation of student ability levels in each class. As a further consequence, students now feel that their maths ability has been determined (i.e. developed a fixed mindset) and teacher expectations have been altered accordingly.To adequately cater for the top students in mixed ability (or indeed streamed) classes, teachers need to reconsider their pedagogy - ensure that the tasks they set up are open-ended and accessible by all students, with opportunity for extension and prompting for those in need.If a goal of maths education is to get students to think like mathematicians and be curious and investigative about the subject, we are definitely doing them a disservice when class groupings serve to encourage a fixed mindset."	1	0	0	3	2.5	3	Education	5200e754ad4a411100000003	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	A1C91EE4289D2BB327C58B7E9B15A1A6	8/6/2013 12:08	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51e7f4ea73317f160000001d	421

"As Jo stated the reasons for low achievement among tracked students, I couldn®t help but recall my experiences in tracked classes where all of these things happened.  Students who were clearly far above the others in terms of their understanding were not challenged at all because the class was taught to the middle and low-achieving students in the class.  The teacher had low expectations of students and often reminded me that we were constrained in what we could teach because they were ™the low kids.š  Students clearly picked up on this and began to have low expectations for themselves as well, not turning in work or completing assignments that they viewed as busywork (because they were!!).	I am currently reading Robyn Jackson®s book, ™Never Work Harder Than Your Students.š  In this book, Jackson discusses the idea of tracking using the analogy of jumping over a rope.  She explains it in the following way: suppose your goal is that students will be able to jump over a rope that is at least two feet off the ground.  If you set up a rope two feet off the ground exactly, the students who can do it immediately will have nothing to do once they jump over it once or twice, and the students who have trouble will continue to struggle with a static, repetitive task.  If you set the rope up seven feet off the ground, you run into the same problem, but this time you have more students struggling and receiving messages that they are ™not good enough.š  If, however, you set up a rope that is two feet off the ground at one end, and 10 feet off the ground at the other, students are able to grow and challenge themselves, no matter what their starting point.  The key with this is that regardless of their starting points, all students are at the very least exposed to the high expectations further down the rope.  Even the students who are working to jump over a two-foot-high rope can anticipate moving along the rope towards the 10-foot end.  It is this heterogeneous grouping, where students® starting points are respected but where all students are still exposed to a challenging environment regardless of their starting point, that leads to the best learning."	1	0	0	4.5	4	2	Education	522943f9999d231200000012	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	9ED8345472CBA9BCAD318DE0019AF4A5	9/6/2013 2:54	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	1	None	10

"I teach in the UK to 11 to 16 yr olds. I have been at this same school for 7 years. Every year group is set by 'ability'. If you are rated as a 3, you are satisfactory but you are made to feel that that is not good enough. Likewise if you are graded a 2, good, you feel you should be achieving a 1, outstanding. Having to fully differentiate every lesson for every class and provide the necessary resources is exhausting. If there was a bank of resources made for every lesson, suitable for every child, it would be possible but there are just not enough hours in the day to create/adapt lessons for everything you could possible need.
