"...when I read some of the discussions below. I get the feeling that there is no flexibility in your school systems (although I don't know where you are all from...). In Sweden there are no national directives about grouping ability. We know from research that heterogeneous groups are preferable, which is why - in the 80s - the Swedish concept of \A school for everyone\"" was planted. Of course, as Jo says, there can be positive things about dividing student in ability groups every now and then, as long as the groups don't stay constant over a longer period of time. At my school, with about 480 students from preschool (6-year-olds) to grade 9, we are working a lot with high expectations, both between leaders-personnel and teachers-students. In math class the teacher often provides problems in different severity or open tasks that can be solved in many different ways and different levels. I would be very surprised if I walked in to a classroom where everybody worked on the same page in the same book. The schedule is flexible to a certain part so that students who need more time to learn basics can get the extra time with a teacher. As for the national tests, these are first of all a possibility for the schools and the teachers, to get a guideline of how well their teaching applies to the rest of the country. NOT to violate the students... The tests are supposed to be done in a way that allows every student to show his or her strengths. Then, of course, the teacher must adjust to each student. I'm sure that this sounds pretentious, and of course we still have a lot to work with when it comes to individualizing at my school as well, but at least we've come a bit on the way. "I am a little nervous about where this bit about \number talks\"" is going because my son had a bad experience with this in 4th and 5th grade. "I often talk about learning synapses and such to my first graders, but what they enjoy most is growing the class brain. At the beginning of the year, I get one of those toy 'grow a brain' (from novelty stores). I talk about how small it is at the beginning of the school year. Then I put it in a vase (ideally one which has a small opening, large middle). Each day a student adds a teaspoon or two of water to represent daily learning. The water enlarges the brain. Truthfully, at the beginning, I sneak a little extra water on it to get it going. During breaks, some water evaporates and the brain can get a bit dirty. I tell the student that the brain did not grow over break because no one was in the class feeding it with learning (water). That's what happens when we don't use our brain and why it is important to continue to learn over vacation time.At the end of the year, it is so big that it won't come out of the vase (why a pear shaped vase it best). "<redacted> brings up an interesting question: what will happen as families are able to chose between schools? Peer effects are important. "I teach in an adult education program that groups students who are working towards their high school equivalency diplomas in the following ways: A. "I read some of the other comments below, and I think there are some very valid points supporting and arguing against heterogenious groups.  I think what is really the most harmful is when there are classes created for heterogenious groups (i.e. the slow class, the gifted class, the average class.) I think students can start to pick up on which students are where and labels are made, strong labels because they were *placed* there.  Clearly, higher powers believe they should be there, so that's pretty dominating and they'll start to limit themselves to that label and belief in themselves (let alone all that was talked about of teacher's not giving the same work or expectations, so they fall more and more behind over time, affecting their future academically forever). "As Cathy introduces the lesson she informs students that they will be working on a multiplication problem.  - They are made aware of what they will be doing.  - She reads the problem out loud and gives them ample time to work on it. - She sees a few thumbs up early and suggests that the early finishers \try to see the problem a different way\"" - She asks them to share their answers. The teacher uses the opportunity to have student think critically. Student recognizes that he is really multiplying by multiples of 10 and not zero and fixes the mistake. The teacher then goes over the correct process once again. - She also repeats what each participating student says, giving the student time to hear and fix their reasoning. - All students are encouraged to participate. "Interesting discussion so far!  I have taught in large comprehensive secondary schools that used grouping by ability level and also small private schools in which the student populations were simply too small to track students.  In the latter case, all students were together and some flexible grouping occurred for core subjects such as reading and maths.  I much preferred teaching in the second environment, primarily because the general ethos of the classes were, on the whole, better.  The lower sets in the first environment tended to be discipline problems and generally, the esteem in which learning was held was much lower.  The higher sets were fun to teach but I don't know that they would have been any less fun if they had included a more comprehensive mix of ability levels.<p>I now live in a small island country and have taught in three different schools here.  In each, classes were mixed, and there may only have been one class at each grade level, so there has been a wide range of ability levels.  These classes have been enjoyable to teach and challenging in a good way.  We are forced, as teachers, to differentiate our lessons, and because we are dealing with students as individuals, we are also forced to continually reassess their skill levels.  Students are not \stuck\"" in one group or another because the teacher is always adjusting his or her perceptions of the students' ability based on current work and progress.  There is generally a more positive view of learning in these classes than in the lower and middle ability groups I have taught previously, and a more cooperative relationships between students and teachers and between students themselves.  When I have taught very low ability groups in the past, I really felt that no matter how much work I put in, I wasn't raising their achievement very much, and their performance on standardized tests certainly bore out my perceptions.  It is very difficult to raise achievement levels in classes where all students have experienced low expectations and low levels of challenge over their whole school careers."""	1	0	0	3.5	2.5	2.5	Education	51fd150453dc971600000015	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	CB526640235A3D0471027DE076CFF75A	8/3/2013 14:34	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	1	51e7f4ea73317f160000001d	421

"Student tracking/grouping has been a hot topic in math for the last several years.  I set my classroom up with students sitting in groups of 3 or 4.  The trick is how do I know what students to sit with whom in order to produce the best results for all students in each group.  Mixing groups with high, middle, middle, low is recommended so that the low student can learn from the high and the high student can teach the low.  The other side of the coin is to group students based upon ability.  The high students sitting all together are suppose to push each other to achieve better and the low students much work to learn since no high student is in the group to give out answers.So what do I do???  I am thinking of putting my students together by current score in my class.  With round of assessment, student groups change.  A student who might have been in the low group one unit of learning can find him/her self in the high group with the next assessment.  I will also be placing the lower groups in the front of the room and the higher groups in the back.  This will also hopefully get the lower groups more engaged in the class since they can no longer hide behind their classmates.  The higher students will continue to vie for teacher attention no matter where they sit.A colleague of mine who use this practice last year, found that her students quickly raised their assessment scores so no one what sitting in the front of the room, directly next to the teacher desk (the low of the lows).  My colleague never told the students how she was seating them, they intuitively figured it out and made sure their personal level of achievement was high enough to keep them away from teacher."	1	0	0	4	2.5	2.5	Education	5224da102c501f1600000001	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	09304A61972C29460FD775DE8C239C2D	9/2/2013 18:33	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	4

"First may I say, I really am beginning to appreciate how forward thinking my school is!We don't stream (possibly an Aussie term but synonymous with tracking or setting) in our school ever, in fact, streaming is a dirty word in the Mathematics department. Instead we work in heterogeneous groups, including in my class at least, one student with learning disabilities that have him working two to four years below the others. We set the students to task and formatively assess those with a particular common error.  We then ask these students to join what we call a fluid group, to focus on this particular area.  Students know that, although they are part of the focus group one lesson that is not likely to be the case the next lesson.  The key is their ability to move between groups.One thing I find though, is that students I now identify as being fixed mindset high achievers, sometimes seem to resent bein given the same materials to work on as the other students.  We  try to stretch these students horizontally rather than vertically.  Ie.  Rather than 'teach them the formulas to remember from the next year's work, which incidentally would not challenge them,we stretch their understanding of the concept by having them explore the overriding concepts and how they can be applied in new and novel ways.  They despise having to explain their understanding and articulate their reasoning, but that is what they are required to do."	1	0	0	3.5	3	3	Education	521347b19d93071600000015	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	63EF576D410BB62A0C26654548F10C47	8/20/2013 10:40	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	10

"I was taught about that similar study Jo mentions about the teacher having higher expectations so the random group of students performing at the top of their peer group when I was in college. It shaped my whole way of thinking and I've been adamantly against ability grouping since I started teaching. Every time it's brought up, I fight it. I have been unsuccessful in fighting ability grouping for 1/2 an hour a day in my building for a language arts piece. In math, however, I chose to ability group when I first started adapting my teaching to allow for more open tasks like the ones we've discussed here in this lesson. I felt that by making smaller groups I would be able to better manage my classroom with minimal chaos as a rookie teacher. My math results were good the first few years and I've received a lot of praise for my math. Unfortunately, it's not my math approach that's being respected, but rather the groups. I stopped doing groups last year as I finally grew comfortable enough to approach open tasks as a whole class and still feel like I was meeting all student needs and I continue to see good scores.Those looking at my classroom continue to neglect the approach I take and continue to think I still ability group. "The elementary school I work at has spent the last couple of years refining our approaches to how we respond and meet the specific needs of students who are \at risk.\"" Our district adopted a pyramid model based on RTI methods - or, Response to Intervention. The pyramid is constructed in 3 parts with the peak representing those student(s) who are receiving services at our school and for what reasons. These services might be reading recovery, resource, or emotional/behavioral counseling. The bottom of the pyramid represents ways in which an individual teacher can meet the needs of a student while in a classroom setting. As you move up the pyramid towards the tip (or, peak), the amounts of one-on-one help sessions with this student will increase, depending on the severity of the students' academic situation. I think the RTI model our school uses provides an example of how we can \""track\"" or monitor student academic progress and in what ways."""	1	0	0	4	2.5	2.5	Education	5200100bcc1dac0e00000073	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	1A97CFBF52BFEF7E75260BFC4BB18C00	8/5/2013 20:50	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	10

"I once had to teach Math to an energetic bunch of 15 year old boys and girls. They were learning about pi. "I've recently challenged myself to group my students randomly each day in math class and have been extremely surprised with the results.  In the past I believed I had to provide everything for my students, constantly monitoring and intervening. "I have very mixed feelings about grouping. I work in a very high achieving public school. However, not every student is super high in math. In my 2nd grade class I had a few students who really needed to be taught the 2nd grade curriculum at a slow pace but a majority of my class understood most of the math concepts without being taught the material. It is really challenging teaching a class that is so differentiated. At my school we begin to group for math starting in 3rd grade. However, the way we group is that we give a pre assessment at the beginning of each topic and the groups are done based on a child's score on the pre assessment. This means that every unit the groups change. I was surprised to see how much they do change each topic. Obviously there are a few kids that stay in the same group for the entire year but it seems that each child excels in a different area of math. I like that they get the opportunity to switch each unit. I think it is easier for teachers because there is a smaller scale of differentiation in each group. "What a fantastic example of teaching to the whole class. "In my school we do not track at all (7th-12th)  However, everyone does not necessarily take calculus.  Students have no choice in their math through grade 10. In grades 11 & 12 they pick classes with guidance from their teachers.  The MA state standards and MCAS test says kids have to be able to solve quadratics.  I personally agree with the person above that I don't believe that to be a necessary skill.  Do all kids need advanced algebra...I don't think so, although my school takes pride in thinking that most of our kids will and should.  If we could take away some of the content expectation and focus on the mathematical thinking, we could more easily group heterogeneously.  When we track, we put kids on a fixed path that due to prerequisites, they can never veer from.  Kids can go down a level, but in math, it is hard to go up a level as usually math is tracked in such a way that kids in upper levels take courses a year early.  So if someone gets stronger in math as they age, they haven't had the prerequisites to move into the upper level without taking a make up course.  With heterogeneous grouping and playing with abilities within a class, all students have the same basic concepts but can develop them to different depths.  If a student better understands one concept over another, they can move more deeply into that concept and spend more time on the basics of another.  Their pacing varies over the course of the year.  The problem right now is that college counselors are pressuring kids to take calculus to be competitive for colleges.  I find myself fighting this constantly with the argument, that I'd rather have the student take a course more suited to their current development and do well, then to take a course that looks challenging on paper only to \fail\"" or feel like they are failing. There is a top-down affect.  High schools want to prepare kids to be successful in college, middle school wants to prepare kids to be successful in high school, etc. But in doing so, we are not necessarily doing what is developmentally appropriate at each grade level.  We need to take their brains where they are and work within the developmental confines of them at that point.  Learning can't take place if the work is too easy OR too hard."""	1	0	0	3.5	2.5	3	Education	5200040fcc1dac0e00000063	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	283FEAD95497B363220EE451B79104E1	8/5/2013 19:59	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51f52c2afa6ce80e00000042	55

"At the small school that I taught at our classes were heterogeneous by necessity. We could only offer one section of each course, based on student numbers. As Dr. Boaler mentioned, this forced us, as teachers, to realize the very different levels present in any one class and teach accordingly. One instructional approach that I found particularly effective was math stations. Math stations are typically used at the elementary level, but they also work REALLY well at the HS level. I was able to differentiate through stations, where students were all working on the same content/concepts, just with different scaffolds available through certain stations. For example, while 5 of the 6 stations were the same for all students, one station offered two \at level\"" and \""above level\"" options for students to consider. "At the end of last year, I happened upon a product in Teachers Pay Teachers called the L.I.N.K. Math Workshop Framework by Colleen Patton.  It is basically a guided math program that uses both whole group, small group, mixed ability and similar ability groupings with rotations.  LINK stands for: L - Learning with manipulativesI - Independent workN - New mathK - Keep it up gamesThis is a very empowering program.  On Mondays, you preview the week.  Then half of the class is doing an extension of previous learning and/or a preassessment of a coming unit while the other half is doing Linking Leaders and Co-leaders, DISCOVERING how to play a new game that they can teach the others.  every day, they all write in their math journals about something they learned that was significant to them.  On Tuesday through Friday, the teacher presents 2-3 minilessons, meet with 2-3 groups, and students will go to a LINK.After analyzing the pre-assessments, the teacher divides the class into two seperate groupings.  The first is a mixed ability group that gets a mini lesson on the current whole group unit of study.  The students are strategically paired so that they have a partner to work with at the independent station, even though they will have different assignments, in case they have questions.  They have the same partner for at least one week.  All students are also grouped into similar ability groups, where the teacher can focus on a common area of need with each group.  There are 4 mixed groups, but only 3 similar ability groups, allowing for one extra session for the similar ability group with the most needs.  These groups are very fluid based on the assessing.  at the end of every lesson cycle (between and after the mixed ability groups and the similar ability groups), there is a check in session with all students at the carpet to talk about their experiences and strategies.  I am just getting ready to implement this, as I see it as a powerful way to implement Rti (Response to Intervention) within my own class.  I feel it is important to give all kids what they need, and this is a way to validate each student.  I was always in higher groups, because we were tracked in high school, but my best friend was in the dummy classes.  They were all given D's to pass and never learned anything.  She didn't know how to make change or multiply or anything when she graduated.  I never want any student of mine to feel useless because all students can reach a level of success"	1	0	0	4.5	3	3	Education	523685fc97adf91200000029	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	583CF181ABC9DD7604F6E5BB9B3EEDBC	9/16/2013 4:15	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	2	None	14

"There are so many enlightening things that Cathy displayed during her number talk. The first was that when she asked the students for answers to the question 25 x 29 and one student gave his answer, Cathy asked if anyone else had a different answer. That is good because some teachers might just start lecturing; however another student said her answer and the first student quickly realized his mistake. This leads into the next thing i noticed. Instead of going forward describing the right answer, Cathy wanted to follow through with how the first student got his incorrect answer. Afterward, cathy acknowledged that the question was hard, mentioned that his thought process was interesting and asked if other students made a similar mistake. I think that during the class discussion acknowledging the question was difficult is a huge deal, because it then makes it ok if someone got the question wrong. Cathy also called the students incorrect thought process \interesting\"" which is much better than say words like \""wrong\"" or \""incorrect\"". Finally, Cathy engages the entire class again by asking if there were similar mistakes made. Later on in the number talk, Cathy asked if any of the students solved the problem in a completely different way and put those answers on the board. Lastly, one thing that stood out to me was when Cathy asked the students to express the different methods in drawings or equations, she asked the students to write on their desks with their fingers. This is a subtle point but it is allowing the students to bring the problem from the abstract word in their minds to the physical world, on the table. "I am a new teacher, so I do have A LOT to learn. However,from my practice teaching experience I learnt a lot. "Although equations can be helpful on all of these, it isn't always necessary.  Here is an example: A collection of 10 coins (all nickels and dimes) is worth 70 cents.  How many of each coin are there?  This could be set up with a system of equations like n + d = 10 and 0.05n + 0.10d = 0.70.  However, we could also do it this way.  If all 10 coins were dimes, we would have $1.00 in coins, but there is 30 cents less than this.  That 30 cent difference is made up by trading in a nickel for a dime. (Remember, we need 10 coins in total.)  Trading one nickel for a dime is a 5 cent difference in coin value.  We need a 30 cent difference in coin value.  30/5 = 6.  So there are 6 nickels and 4 dimes.  No \algebra\"" necessary."""	0	0	0	4	3.5	2.5	Education	520150d5ad4a410e0000005c	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	A6A08E7FD0D90A7935C9D795815FB87E	8/6/2013 19:39	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	1	None	53

"First of all, you have used the procedural method that requires learning to use and compute with formulas. You found slope, then used the point-slope formula to write an equation and computed the value of y. It is utilization of particular rules, algorithms and procedures. This is also called the functional approach in learning algebra, because you have used a rate of change and variation. Your second approach where you had to look at the figures and generalize is a structural method. It is focused om underlying structure and patterns. You have moved away from the contextual problem and developed ability to generalize the patterns using different ways and following procedures in a systematic way to get the formula. You have been developing or discovering the relationships and no formulas have been given. "I would start the year by doing a very simple problem for the students and making a mistake on the problem. "I teach at a small high school.  The students are grouped by math ability in that most freshman take Algebra, unless they were \tracked\"" into algebra in middle school and then they take Geometry as a Freshman. Co-op students (with IEPs or 504s) are also with the general population. There is no other (lower)  math choices, all students take Algebra. "Girls and students of colour in this research have more of a likelihood for developing a fixed mindset in their formative years. The interventions work most with these groups for the statistical reason that these form the greatest subset of students with the less desired mindset. The experiences for this are varied, but at some level it must include the 'following of rules', with this group choosing the path \IF (action) THEN (success)\"" believing the only other path to be \""IF (not action) THEN (notsuccess)\"" rather than exploring other possibilities for example \""IF(Not Action) THEN (success)\"". "Schools will, I have no doubt, have the self perception that they already take on the growth mindset, even before this new evidence was produced; which school would say otherwise? Every school that I have been involved in has tracking systems monitoring the progress of students, incorporates minimum levels of expected progress over five years, one year, six weekly on which the teacher, department and school has to report back where targets have been met or otherwise. This alone indicates that they believe that students should make progress. The structure within mathematics for progress is based upon the 'ladder' which Paul Lockhart so eloquently  describes at the end of his 'Lament' essay. This is the working context that schools choose to work in, and so the growth mindset has to be linked to achieving the next level or grade. To remove this constraint in our present context may only improve the growth of  a few whilst marginalising the majority, whose motivational reality remains the 'grade'. As it stands in the UK, schools now have the choice to adapt the curriculum to their own needs; I would like to see mathematics departments reduce the ratio of objectives to time, in order to explore and develop the range of mathematical experiences for each objective, whilst still maintaining the 'reality of grades', to improve the learning of mathematics."	1	0	0	4	3.5	2	Education	5201fcc9ad4a4111000000df	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	6E04BA82450553DE0C60CDB32FCA36DE	8/7/2013 7:52	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	31

"I substitute teach and I want to share an experience I had in 3rd grade, several years ago. "I always like to emphasize with my students that mistakes are how we learn. At the start of the school year, we discuss the fact that if none of us made mistakes, then we really wouldn't need to be in school because we'd all be perfect!  Therefore, mistakes are encouraged and analyzed together so we can learn. I take the pressure off individual students by shifting the paradigm. Instead of, \What mistakes did some of you make on this problem?\"" I ask, \""What are some common errors students might make on a problem like this one?\"" This allows students to discuss frequent errors without feeling any sense of ownership or embarrassment from a mistake.  Once we have developed the culture, most students openly own their mistakes and gladly share so others can learn from them."""	1	0	0	4	3.5	2	Education	51ecb128205b020a00000078	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	C799AA524B7C4AB112F9985DA588DAF0	7/22/2013 4:12	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	1	None	17

"Our school has been experimenting with different models of grouping students.When we had mixed ability groups I can say that it didn't work well - lower achieving students lacked the confidence and belief that they could achieve more highly then they expected.  They became frustrated and disruptive.  This is probably due to them having already been labelled 'low ability'.  The higher achieving students soon ran out of material and some would sit, after they had finished their exercises content to do nothing else.  The problem here seems to be the tasks that we have given the students - not open enough.  In order to begin to teach students in a mixed group you would need to do an immense amount of groundwork, giving them confidence, training them in how to be more independent and self-starting, preparing the kind of tasks during a lesson that ALL of them could do and still learn from.A second type of grouping we tried with lots more success was based on a pre-assessment.  This would be done several times during the year.  The pre-assessment would indicate a general aptitude (eg, with algebra, number, data or shape) and we would group the students based on this.  However, the students would still know whether they were in the top or bottom group so I imagine that this would promote a fixed mindset too.I want to have my students in mixed groups - the research indicates that this is the best thing to do after all.  The difficulty is HOW then do I teach them?  The ability range is so vast on occasions.  Perhaps you could also say that their learning styles are also far apart (I suspect that the 'high achievers' are more passive, are able to concentrate, do not mind sitting still, whereas the 'low achievers' are more active, want to be up out of their seats, chatting, playing, doing). I like to use a partner wheel in math class for group work.  I divide the class in half with the strongest students names going on the outside of a circle and the other half going around the inside of the circle. This is fastened with a brass fastener. "\Coasting\"" is what I call this behavior. Some students do it all of the time, and all students do it some of the time.And, it's true, an outside observer can't tell what's going on in such a student's brain. Plus, all brains need to coast now and then -- learning isn't necessarily about being intense or ultra-focused or good at giving speeches.Some students are shy, or receiving messages that damage their self-esteem from somewhere outside the class, and a class where participation is forced can be painful to them and make them retreat further.Here's where teaching experience can help the teacher gain enough sensitivity to know when to engage a particular student or students and when to let them observe and tag along. If the teacher gives the student a little leeway, the student may well gain comfort and start participating on his or her own. On the other hand, sometimes the teacher needs to say \""Here, do this\"" without giving the student time to object -- cutting through whatever is blocking the student's participation.Students are used to these peer group situations where some members of the group are seldom active participants and where some are having a bad day -- teachers can learn a lot by paying attention to how students relate to each other within a group.A teacher can also talk about \""coasting\"" and what is an expected and useful degree of participation."""	1	0	0	4	4	2	Education	5209721584e4c61200000001	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	CF57D72790976294EA7793E247008661	8/12/2013 23:39	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	3	51eb876c0ad94c0a00000069	203

"One way to group my students that I found to be effective for both quick learners and those who need more time to learn is that I pair these learners together.  So, there is one quick and one slower learner paired together.  Usually the quick learner has quickly completed the task, but because their partner is not able to solve it as quickly, it causes the quick learner to slow down, reprocess what was done, and then explain it to their partner.  Then the slower learner is able to hear how the problem was solved, talk it over with their partner, and try to solve in the same way, or perhaps in a different way.  Then both partners come up in front of the class and must each explain one portion of how they solved the problem.  This helps both my learners to do the work and feel responsible.  When they solve it incorrectly, it puts it back on both of them to work together, instead of feeling like they solved it incorrectly because they are in a \low\"" group or incapable."""	1	0	0	4.5	3.5	2	Education	51eeff577446c40a000000b6	Education/EDUC115N/How_to_Learn_Math	06A6D499B656D0904C6DD06A78EE7D33	7/23/2013 22:10	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	14

"In the early 1990s, there was a theory that cold baths might help individuals with chronic fatigue syndrome (also known in the UK as ME or myalgic encephalomyelitis). I think it was put forward by a reputable medical doctor, I think Dr Vijay Kakkar. You had to sit in a cold bath every 1 or 2 days I think, with the duration of sitting in there extending by 1 or 2 minutes each time. I think the theory was to do with resetting or influencing the hypothalamus.It was a bit controversial with people worrying that sitting already ill people in cold water could make things worse for them. But a few people, including the Dr himself I think, said it was beneficial for them. Others didn't find it helpful. It doesn't seem to have caught on or been researched much more since as far as I can tell from a quick search on the internet.However, there was one aspect that always intrigued me. I tried the method myself for a few weeks and I noticed that about 3-4 hours after getting out of the cold bath I would experience a sudden intense rush of warmness all over my body for a couple of minutes. It was a bit like a hot flush I imagine, though it was not uncomfortably hot and did not provoke sweating. It was so noticeable that the first time I looked round to see if other people had also just experienced something changing in the environment, only to realize that it was only me. It was actually quite nice, an extremely cozy sort of warmth - so nice it would have been lovely if it had continued for longer. This occurred despite the fact that I had never felt cold after getting dressed from the bath and had been feeling warm and in a perfectly warm environment for at least 2-3 hours before the warm surge arrived. And the timing was remarkably predictable. "In the mini-lecture about Cory's body temperature, \after-drop\"" was explained to occur because vasoconstriction had drawn blood away from the extremities and into the core while Cory was in the cold water bath. "Hello everyone,just as a small FYI i'd like to write a few words about **post-operative shivering**.Sometimes patients experiment shivering in the post operative care unit. This phenomenom is rather complex. As an anesthesiologist i would say that shivering is not associated with any big issues.The pathophysiology is hard to understand. **Some patients are really hypothermic, **some others not**.** Anesthetic drugs impairs hemodynamics and the reactivity of the smooth muscle of the vessels leading to redistribution of cold blood from the periphery to the central core. The surgery (cardiac surgery +++) may generate a burst of inflammation and some chemical messengers (pro inflammatory cytokines) trigger shivering. There are also some hypotheses discussing an offset in the hypothalamus sensors and some complex nervous uncoupling between the cortex and the medulla.There are a lot of efficient drugs and strategies to prevent and treat this phenomenom so if you have experiment it or if you are scheduling for a surgery you can ask your anesthetist about his strategy to manage this.Rémi, french anesthetist"	1	0	0	4.5	2.5	3.5	Humanities	52d66161c2cb34bee800002b	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	C6FFF6B5AF9A86695F690B728925BB51	1/15/2014 10:22	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	44

"Hi there. Not yet doing the homework, haha; but i have some ideas about your discussion.I don't think the subject will use less oxygen. The adaptation in athletes come to happen in the hearth, reducing the cardiac frequence and sometimes even increasing the size of the hearth; this is because the constant hypoxia in the working muscles makes the capillaries to increase their numbers, so in a relaxed situation there's more perfussion, so the same oxygen (or even more if the energy requirement of the muscles increase due to hypertrofia) travels the circulatory system in less time and more efficiently, so the heart has to work less.The metabolism adaptation you mention, i don't know if you meant a mollecular level, but i don't think that's the case. There's no way to improve the chemical reactions required to synthetize ATP; in fact the only way for the mitochondria to adapt is to increase the enzymes required for the synthesis and with that the oxygen requirement also increases. In a chronic cold adaptation, that's what happen, the mitochondria makes more and more reactions so the number of enzymes increases, the requirement of oxygen increases and the respiratory frequency increases. It might happen, just as the adaptation to high altittude, that the chronic hypoxia increases the number of red cells and capillaries, so the gas exchange in the lungs becomes more efficient, and this way the respiratory frequency can drop, even though the oxygen consumption increases.Well, anyway, I hope this is useful. Sorry for bad english, haha. "My take on this - The sequence was planned out for the experiment from water to treadmill (not for exposure but for the evaluation of effect of exercise on core temperature). Initially the core temperature is maintained (whether water or air or under snow) by Vascular Regulation. This will happen for a shorter time of exposure and in Corey's case he was removed from the water after a while to avoid the stage where his core temp starts to drop.When on the treadmill, Corey's core temperature started to drop drastically as the blood flow increased to his active limbs - legs, arms etc. This forced the vascular regulation to allow blood to the muscles under exercise. The feeling of cold intensified, resulting in shivering and of course there was faster drop in core temperature.However, your conclusion is correct that the loss of heat is faster in water than air. This being a controlled experiment, it did not come out that way."	1	0	1	4	1.5	3.5	Humanities	52d694588fbbc65896000037	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	7B90784F92240374088B60E5423FF6B5	1/15/2014 13:59	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	1	52d682d2c2cb34c96c000031	46

"EP101 Staff: Interesting discussion.  It is true that the impact of heat loss through the head had been exaggerated for years - it use to be thought that 80% of body heat was lost through the head, which is not true.  Still, it remains a major source of heat loss.  As an appendage sticking out in the cold with lots of blood vessels that you can't constrict (because your brain would not be happy with that), there is heat lost to the environment. Hair helps, but a good hat helps more. If you are out in the cold, carrying or using a hat makes sense, just like having gloves and keeping your chest covered. "Staff: What Marc says above is correct.  We do lose heat through our hands and feet especially in the heat. "I read a study done recently which debunked the theory that most of our body's heat loss was through the head. Because our face, head and chest are more sensitive to changes in temperature than the rest of the body, when we cover them up it makes it feel like we are doing more to prevent heat loss. When in fact, covering one part of the body has as much effect as covering another. The belief that most of our heat loss is through our head is based on a study that was done in the 1950's. A more recent study determined no more than 10% of our body's heat loss is through the head."	1	0	0	4	3.5	2.5	Humanities	52d70943ba32197eb2000024	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	204C7203BCF31A03BECC273B427E67A2	1/15/2014 22:18	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	52d478424c121b91af00003e	143

Sweating is determined by the amount of evaporative heat loss required to reach heat balance (i.e. the difference between heat production and all non-evaporative sources of heat loss) and sweating efficiency (i.e. the ratio between evaporated sweat and secreted sweat - some of which drips off the skin or gets trapped in clothing contributing nothing to heat loss). "Conductive heat transfer was not mentioned as a mechanism of afterdrop in the lectures but found here:http://www.ebmedicine.net/topics.php?paction=showTopicSeg&topic_id=37&seg_id=694It seems reasonable that both (convective and conductive) mechanisms might be in play.\Conductive heat transfer offers an alternative explanation for observed afterdrop. "Interesting riddle. Here's my thoughts. Your base layer was cotton, which doesn't wick sweat away from your skin at all because it is hydrophillic and easily absorbs water. Your second layer, wool, was a good insulator (a common insulator like fleece) to the point that it caused you to perspire. Your perspiration could not be wicked away from your skin. Both the moisture trapped on your skin as well as that moisture being exposed to the air lowered your body temperature. When you removed the sweater, you were no longer so warm that you perspired leaving no moisture directly on the skin. So, even though you had a loose cotton T-shirt as your base layer, there was no moisture trapped on the skin being exposed to air. As such, you felt warmer without the wool insulator. My last thought, if you felt warmer without the wool vs with the wool but still felt cold overall, using a better base layer than a cotton shirt would have made all the difference. I know a lot about snow-sport base layers due to snowboarding but was surprised that there are base layers made specifically for motorcyclists that are both wicking and tight fitting, which would keep moisture off your skin and increase that air pocket you were talking about."	1	0	0	4	4	2.5	Humanities	52d78bac80828454ad00001c	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	E52AF10538729ED9E8D9A272BB41E6B2	1/16/2014 7:35	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	52d574497214195d2e000015	52

"From what I understand, a lot of research is going on in this field right now- how to make additional BAT, how to change beige adipose to brown, etc. Researchers have succeeded in growing mature human brown fat cells from preadipocytes that were taken from a fresh sample of brown fat from a patient having neck surgery. From what I have read, researchers haven’t found a way yet to essentially “make” more BAT. BAT is able to produce large amounts of heat through activation of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1). When UCP1 is activated, it allows a free-flow of protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, resulting in the rapid release of chemical energy as heat. BAT is most abundant in adults in the deep regions of the neck and chest- close to the sympathetic chain and carotid arteries where is can quickly warm the blood and raise core body temperature.When rolling in the snow or taking cold showers (cold-induced thermogenseis), I believe the theory is not to make new BAT but to activate the adults current stores of BAT. When it is cold out, or your body gets cold your core temperature drops. Your muscles help raise your core temp by shivering. Your body’s thermoregulatory functions activate BAT which activates UCP1 thus releasing chemical energy as heat. This process burns white adipose tissue, improves blood circulation and increases your metabolism theoretically helping you to lose weight."	0	0	0	4	4	2.5	Humanities	52d8b7271753e964c800000d	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	7512F3073AA3FFCB8DE24287D86ACA51	1/17/2014 4:52	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	2	52d73ccb80828454ad000010	54

"Staff: You bring up an interesting dilemma that happens frequently in physiology: sacrificing something longer term for immediate survival.  By increasing the activity of BAT, you do burn more calories which could be a problem down the road, but you need additional heat right now!  If you didn't increase metabolic rate and increase heat production, core temperature would fall more and you would get hypothermic faster.  At least, by keeping you warm in the short-term, you have a chance of getting rescued and eating more food in the future.  If you die sooner from hypothermia by saving your energy for later, that doesn't help much. There are lots of other examples of this in the body, such as breaking down lean mass to supply short term energy supplies when your carbohydrate stores are depleted during exercise. "Remember, we're looking for the beta that minimizes RSS.  Now, let's say I add one more game, game n+1, which is played between Weber State (let's call them team 1) and some new team, team p+1.  The claim is that (beta hat 1, ..., beta hat p) are going to be the same before and after I add this data point.Here's why: for *any* setting of beta hat 1, I can set beta hat (p+1) so my model perfectly predicts game n+1.  Because beta hat (p+1) only affects one game, that is exactly what I'll do.But then, minimizing RSS over all n+1 games just reduces to minimizing RSS over the first n games, and then choosing beta hat (p+1) to make the last residual 0."	0	0	0	4	3	3.5	Humanities	52d9c0322849c067ad000026	HumanitiesScience/Stats216/Winter2014	1537B1A0B9A589ADF7CCF6599B0B2E85	1/17/2014 23:43	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	1	52d993a12849c0c436000018	113

"Remember that thermal energy is just the sum of the kinetic energy of all molecules of the body.Aimeceleste is right. Each time a molecule from the air or from the water hits a molecule from your body (which is also in movement), your body's molecule transfers a little kinetic energy to the air molecule. This happens a LOT of times per second, making the total energy loss considerable.So, the higher the density, more molecules to bump into you!That also explains why the wind takes heat more efficiently. As the air is moving faster, the microscopic colisions are happening much faster. The same would happen if you were underwater in a place with water current.Generalizing, the heat loss depends on your body size, the density and speed of the fluid you are in."	0	0	1	4	3.5	2.5	Humanities	52dacc3429555a7c98000008	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	2AE9FE41AFEFDE90801AC4E14FB3700D	1/18/2014 18:47	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	52d9a4be2849c067ad00001e	28

"Q: At the same submaximal workload on an exercise bike before and after endurance training, you will use:A: The same amount of oxygen.The concept of a submax workload and oxygen consumption is tricky, and often students in our class at Stanford have trouble with it before it clicks. So know your confusion is in good company. Lets see if I can be helpful. The main point is this: **it requires the same amount of oxygen for your body to do a certain amount of work.** If that work is below the maximal capacity, we call it a submax workload. For example, I did a few months of cycling training to increase my aerobic fitness a year or so back as a part of a previous teaching project. We tested my VO2max by doing a progressive (increasing workload every few minutes) test on a stationary bike where I wore a mask that measured the oxygen I was using at Week 0, Week 5, and Week 10 of my training regimen. My VO2max increased across my 10 week training program because my body had optimized components of the fick equation, meaning that I could finish the test at a later stage where I cycled at higher watts of resistance. Lets say at Week 0 my maximum resistance at the end of the test was 250 watts, but at Week 10 it was 350 watts. Because of my training, I was becoming a better cyclist! Here is the point. Regardless of my training and assuming my cycling technique didn't change, at 150 watts (a light, submaximal workload), my body needed to consume the same amount of oxygen at Week 0 Week 5 and Week 10 to do 150 watts of work. The difference is, at the end of the training, my body could consume more oxygen, and 150 watts of a submaximal workload was easier because it was a lower percentage of my overall VO2max. -Staff"	0	0	1	4	2	3	Humanities	52daf2850283d0a438000012	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	499E88807DA7733E349062678EE8B7AA	1/18/2014 21:30	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	1	52d8f5f52849c0635b000002	115

"Immersion in a tepid bath had long been the accepted means, along with medication, of quickly reducing dangerously high fevers in infants and toddlers in the ED. The primary problem with this method was that the children/ infants usually responded to the immersion with heat generating behaviors such as vigorous flailing about in the water and nonstop crying. In an attempt to eliminate, or minimize this counterproductive behavior, we began to drape our little patients with wet towels and place a fan in front of them. This evaporative cooling method proved very successful. The infants and children usually remained calm and fever reduction occurred even more rapidly than with the immersion method. Also, with our patients in a calm state, it was easier to notice when they began to shiver, thus signaling when to stop the cooling measure. Another indirect benefit of the evaporative cooling method was that parents were more willing to do this at home, if necessary, because they were much less likely to have to deal with a screaming, stressed out infant."	0	0	1	4	3.5	2.5	Humanities	52db02aa9e322a9641000022	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	94810D3A08ED85E36F6A5A01933B2F30	1/18/2014 22:39	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	17

"Non-shivering thermogenesis (NST) is a heat-production mechanism participating in the chemical thermoregulation of mammals.2. NST is additional to shivering and takes place at temperatures close to the thermoneutral zone.3. NST occurs in newborn mammals and in those that hibernate. In some adult mammals it can be induced by adaptation to cold.4. In small mammals NST produces approximately the same amount of heat as shivering. It becomes less important with increasing body weight of the animals.5. NST is regulated by the hypothalamus and it is based predominantly on the calorigenic action of noradrenaline released from sympathetic nerve-endings.Participation of other calorigenic substances and of the specific dynamic action of food cannot be excluded.6. NST is localized mainly in skeletal muscles and in brown adipose tissue. Small amounts of NST may come from liver, intestine, heart and brain.7. The biochemical basis of the calorigenic action of noradrenaline has not yet been fully elucidated"	0	0	1	4	2.5	2.5	Humanities	52dbdf3a89ad5c9c3e000018	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	26F30D3F3929FB483ED518A9E4C2D4D2	1/19/2014 14:20	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	52dbd66f9fb07319e2000007	36

"In a few words, we lose heat through four processes: radiation, convection, conduction, and evaporation. We want to minimize all four losses. Being with an outer insulation that shelters the body from wind, cold rain, and other external conditions that may take away heat from the body. (In lay person terms, keep the cold out.) Thereafter, dress in layers, keeping in mind that each layer is an insulator onto its own, plus the airgap in between also further insulates. Finally, the base layer, the layer closest to your skin, should fit snuggly against your skin. It should also wick away your perspiration. As we learned in this section, wet perspiration will conduct heat away from your body faster than simple cold air. Personally for the base layer I prefer polypropylene fiber materials, but you can also use silk, which is deliciously oh-so-expensive.There are other considerations to take into account in addition to thermal insulation, including mobility, cost, and of course appearance!"	1	0	0	4	2.5	2.5	Humanities	52dbfaf4d149d1e416000007	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	415EC59D4C27FD534D2FECF5B44A4674	1/19/2014 16:19	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	52dba814c0111667ca000017	31

"When we are too cold the blood vessels supplying warm blood to the skin become narrow or constrict (vasoconstriction). This reduces the flow of warm blood near the surface of the skin, and reduces heat loss.This is why some people's skin looks paler when they feel too cold.A very common mistake in exams is to write that the blood vessels move up and down in the skin. The blood vessels do not move during vasodilation and vasoconstriction.Controlling temperatureToo cold	Too hot![enter image description here][1]![enter image description here][2]Diagram shows cross section of skin when cold, with erect hairs (B) caused by tense hair muscles (A), and reduced blood flow to capillaries (C)	Diagram shows a cross section of skin when hot. Hair muscles relax (D) causing hairs to lie flat so that heat can escape. Sweat is secreted (E) from the sweat glands. Blood flow in the capillaries is increased (F)A - Hair muscles pull hairs on end.B - Erect hairs trap air.C - Blood flow in capillaries decreases.	D - Hair muscles relax. Hairs lie flat so heat can escape.E - Sweat secreted by sweat glands. Cools skin by evaporation.F - Blood flow in capillaries increases.Signals along nerves from the hypothalamus control both vasodilation and vasoconstriction.Muscles attached to our skeleton can also receive signals from the hypothalamus when we feel too cold. They respond by shivering. The rapid contraction of muscles during shivering results in heat being produced during respiration. "Staff: Hello Everyone, Nice work catching our attention with all your great posts!  You have the right idea on the theory of ice bath: reduced inflammation, increased constriction, followed by increased flow to the tissues (called reactive hyperemia:  when the circulation is slowed or cut off to an area the blood then returns afterwards at a higher rate to flush out waste products and deliver nutrients).  You are also accurate in your discussion of the mixed results.  Despite the fact that some athletes and coaches swear by it, there is no consistent data that suggests that it is better than other (less painful) cool downs - such as a light active cool down.  IF you have an actual injury than the reduction in inflammation can be beneficial, but you'd could also achieve that with a more localized application of cold.  Having said that though, there are a lot of things out there that seem to work for individuals that are hard to support with scientific data - meaning when you combine a group together, the positive, neutral and negative responders cancel each other out. I'm not great in the cold, so I personally would not suffer through it for the degree of benefit that has been indicated. But, if you think it is working for you, I wouldn't stop doing it either. Sorry if that sounds wishy washy, but sometimes in physiology the individual response is the most important. You will find that is true for altitude training as well.  It seems to work for some, but not others (although in that case we have a slightly better idea of why...).  If you are a positive responder then altitude training can give you that 2% benefit you need. If you are not, it could actually make you worse. Keep up the great discussions. There are a lot of very well informed people out there!"	1	0	1	5	1	4.5	Humanities	52dc46bbd149d1ec3d000011	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	261F8F6E8B46A29D1D12E5CB0E262DD9	1/19/2014 21:42	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	8	52d927672849c0c436000007	455

"For 25 summers my family lived in Yellowstone National Park where my husband worked as a seasonal park ranger. Here is a little \cold\"" adventure we had there when our children were in their early teens.On an end of the summer outing with our 24' sailboat on Yellowstone Lake, we were caught by an unexpected \""Nor'easter\"" that was bringing an early fall snowstorm to the park. As the winds increased, the mooring lines were snapping and the dock was breaking apart. My husband and son started the motor and our daughter and I cast of the remaining lines so they could take the boat out, to avoid having it dashed to pieces on shore by the wind waves. Then my daughter and I crawled back to shore on the violently bucking dock, as parts of it were snapping and breaking off.We didn't know how long we would be there, so we decided to set up a small shelter and make a little fire using twigs and dead branches. We always carried a small waterproof container of matches for just such an emergency. The air temperature probably dropped to the low 50's and the wind was really blowing hard. We were discussing whether we would need to spend the night in the outhouse as we sat shivering by our little fire, trying to warm our hands and dry our socks, when we heard someone calling us from afar. It was my husband and son in our boat! "I wanted to also voice my appreciation for the story-based approach. I find it very effective.I've been involved in teaching rock climbing merit badge to boy scouts this last year. "Let's say you have a high test error and you would like to reduce it.So you should compare test error with train error.1. If train error is high, you have high bias. It is also known as underfitting. It means you are using too simple (not flexible) model. So you should try to use more complex (flexible) model. For example, you have high bias if you are trying to fit quadratic function with linear regression.2. If train error is low, then you have high variance. It is also known as overfitting. It means you are using too complex (flexible) model. So you should try to use more simple (not flexible) model. Also, you should definitely have a look at https://class.coursera.org/ml-003/lecture/62"	0	0	1	4	3	2.5	Humanities	52dfc2947ebe329f2200006c	HumanitiesScience/StatLearning/Winter2014	9CC891EC189DAFFF959F7291004AE302	1/22/2014 13:07	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	19	52dfb1967ebe329f22000065	1096

"The way I understand it is that the bias is how \rigid\"" your model is. So if you have a linear model, the relationship can only be linear. Even if the true function is quadratic, you have a bias for being linear since you can't match the points that are not aligned in a straight line. If you go to a quadratic model, you increase your flexibility (and reduce your linear bias) and you can match more points. If you take this to the extreme and create a model so flexible that it will match every test point individually (like the KNN=1 in the examples) the variance of your model is increased as you will be matching more of the noise and less of the signal. Does that make sense?"""	0	1	0	3	5.5	4.5	Humanities	52e077ac30d21b40eb00005d	HumanitiesScience/StatLearning/Winter2014	395646B7EDB326AFF5F6E5001B313E6B	1/23/2014 2:00	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	3	52e025ca30d21b89df000025	558

"Below is a reference to pursue learning a bit more about BAT. The function of brown adipose tissue is to turn food into heat, and it does so by this particular mechanism- uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation. Basically, harnessing the energy gradient produced by metabolism and turning it into heat instead of into chemical energy to be used for work. As we learned from Anne, these metabolic reactions that turn our food into chemical energy  are all inefficient, releasing some heat in the process. But these brown adipose tissues are particularly specialized to be able to uncouple oxidative phosphorylation- to be less efficient at creating chemical energy and better instead at producing heat. -staffGeneral Information on BAT from 2004 paper:http://physrev.physiology.org/content/84/1/277.shortKahn academy short video on Oxidative Phosphorylation and chemiosmosis. "Staff: Scott, This is a great question and it I had to think about it a moment.  I like the way you are able to integrate physiology concepts with your question.  I believe that there is not a large decrease in the (a-v)O2 because most of the oxygen is being extracted by the working muscles during exercise.  The constriction to the periphery that is taking place is to the tissues that are not active (e.g. your arms and hands when you are running).  The working muscles will have local tissue vasodilators such as CO2, Nitric oxide, K+, adenosine, higher temperatures, etc. that keep the flow coming to where it is needed. Also, it is possible that the VO2 of the muscles may actually go up slightly.  If you believe that maximal oxygen consumption is limited by delivery rather than extraction, then directing more blood to the working muscles and less to peripheral inactive tissues could actually increase VO2 and work capacity of the active muscles (sort of the reverse of adding arm cranking during max VO2 of the legs - resulting in the same whole body VO2max, but lower work output of the legs). So, to answer your question, I think the math still works and you could get an increase in VO2max in the cold, but the difference would be small. Thanks for all your great posting on the forum. Keep it up!"	0	0	1	4	1.5	2	Humanities	52e159374c46c4aea400000b	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	261F8F6E8B46A29D1D12E5CB0E262DD9	1/23/2014 18:02	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	52dec66c53cc44ffe50000ab	37

"Good question, I would think BP decreasesa ctually. My reasoning (please someone comment!):Cardiac output is a measure of how much blood volume is pumped out from the heart per minute. As such it depends on the stroke volume and the heart rate (beats per minute). In this question we know that cardiac output is decreased due to decreased stroke volume (and assuming that the heart rate is not compensating enough by beating faster).Now blood pressure measures the force the blood pumped exerts on the arterial walls. This depends on the cardiac output obviously, but also rheological factors related to the properties of blood (eg viscosity) and the vessel wall (eg elasticity). So I guess the answer to your questions will depend on how the other factors change... If you assume that during a short term acute heat exposure where as per the answer to 2.4 the heart rate is not elevated, and that other factors don't change, then a decreased cardiac output will mean a decrease in BP."	1	0	1	4	1.5	2.5	Humanities	52e2f1696f89431ac6000045	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	4204AE3E4E8799EF2D1AC64979664BC1	1/24/2014 23:04	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	52df6a407ebe32732900005a	43

"Ah, the frequentist vs. bayesian interpretations of confidence intervals!Short answer: neither interpretations suggest a 95% probability of truth for the parameter.Long answer: read on.For the frequentist, there is only one true value for the parameter, which is hidden and we can only approximate based on theories like the Central Limit Theorem. Note that with each random sample set, we expect to get different confidence intervals. Hence, the 95% confidence interval for a parameter indicates that if we repeated the fitting using multiple (& infinite) number of random sample sets, 95% of confidence intervals produced would contain the true parameter. For the bayesian, the parameter (or its estimate) is random and has an associated probability distribution. The 95% **credible** interval communicates the level of belief the experimenter has of the parameter i.e. she is 95% sure of the parameter estimate. Note that it is a subjective belief as the interval is of the posterior distribution based on the experimenter's chosen prior. So, if you're not confused by now, you haven't understood it. In practise, most decisions are made as you suggested: 95% probability the true parameter lies within the interval. Nothing bad has happened yet, well maybe the GFC."	0	0	1	4	3.5	2	Humanities	52e3ffc5df09ce4adf000034	HumanitiesScience/StatLearning/Winter2014	2B4031CA5CFD2104E18F7D2316661335	1/25/2014 18:17	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	22	52e3f583df09ce4adf00002f	2846

"There are two functions that are not to be confused. One is the ultimate function you are trying to arrive to that is used to predict Y as a function of X. The other function is MSE as a function of the coefficients of X which you are trying to minimize. The first function can be non-linear in X so that it can take complex shapes, but the model is linear in the parameters (coefficients) that you are trying to fit, this way you can simply walk down the gradient towards the point that minimizes MSE. You can then take the best values of coefficients and plug them into f-hat.So, to reiterate, for the fitting step your coefficients are the variables, once you found the best value of the coefficients they become constants in the main function which is a function of X."	0	0	1	4	2.5	2.5	Humanities	52e483ecde09290e5d00003a	HumanitiesScience/StatLearning/Winter2014	DD46CA1743C452FED84C26CB6E8F320C	1/26/2014 3:41	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	2	52e47807b945eb274f00004c	405

"In another course I took, it was recommended to try to tailor the flexibility of your approach to the amount of training data you have. The rule of thumb was to try to pick your model so that the number of training data points are in the region of around ten times the VC dimension of the model (the VC dimension corresponds roughly to the number of free parameters in the model). Having this number of points or more is usually (but not always) OK, but if you have less you might get in trouble.However, this is just a rule of thumb. It is useful to rule out models that are too flexible and are unlikely to work with the data resources you have. "I think the point of this question is to show that the method of nearest neighbors breaks down when p is very large. If this were not the case, the method of nearest neighbors would be used quite often as it comes very close to the \gold standard\"", the Bayes classifier, with respect to test error rate. The error rate of the Bayes classifier is analogous to the irreducible error, which is the portion of test MSE we cannot model. (See page 39 for a discussion of this.) Of course, this depends on the choice of k which optimizes the bias-variance tradeoff. Also, like linear regression, the nearest neighbor classifier can be used with either quantitative or qualitative responses and the result is easy to interpret. In addition, the nearest neighbor method can perform similarly or better than linear regression for both prediction and inference dependent on the true form of the function. In the case of inference, nearest neighbors can perform better as the real world is not usually linear.   Low test error rate, useful with both quantitative and qualitative responses for both prediction and inference, and simple to interpret are all desirable traits of a good statistical learning method."""	1	0	0	4	2.5	4	Humanities	52e53000a8d51bc13d000005	HumanitiesScience/StatLearning/Winter2014	03E82BA9EFAF6DF346F8F5A8FEB6D367	1/26/2014 15:55	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	4	52df0138182f4b0ffc000019	4256

"Hi Tara, my sense is that shifting to a human rights or social justice lens helps to frame issues that affect women in a way that emphasizes their rights (and, in some ways, their existence) as individuals that a development lens does not. "I want to begin with a brief examination of the language used in the “United Nations Declaration of Human Rights.” I believe that language matters and that the way that issues are spoken about has demonstrable consequences on the way we think and act within our social worlds. "Security Council Resolution 1325 was passed unanimously on 31 October 2000. It invited Secretary-General Kofi Annan to carry out a study on the impact of armed conflict on women and girls, the role of women in peace-building and the gender dimensions of peace processes and conflict resolution. Resolution (S/RES/1325) is the first resolution ever passed by the Security Council that specifically addresses the impact of war on women, and women's contributions to conflict resolution and sustainable peace. The Security Council was concerned about civilians in armed conflict, particularly women and children, who constituted most of the victims and were increasingly targeted by armed elements. "The Treaty provides an international standard for protecting and promoting women’s human rights and is often referred to as a “Bill of Rights” for women.The International Convention to Eliminate All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) enshrines these rights-and recognizes that women and girls often face challenges to realizing their rights specific to their gender. As such, CEDAW urges an equitable approach to human rights, recognizing the range of gender-specific human rights violations, ranging from sex slavery to maternal mortality to property and inheritance rights. CEDAW is an effective tool for women to advocate for their own rights and a standardized benchmark to which all countries should aspire. . It is the only international instrument that comprehensively addresses women’s rights within political, civil, cultural, economic, and social life. "I was trying to calculate VIF manually, so I could get a better feel for it - I was confused by the definition on the book, I am not saying it is not clear, just that I did mot understand it. I try to understand the concepts versus just memorize them and was looking to get an 'intuition' for it (I took the Stamford ML class as well and Professor Ng always talked about the intuition, which worked for me)I did some digging and this is how one can do it, for those who may be interested in understanding itFollowing the example from the book to fit the model (as an R formula): balance ~ age + rating + limit say we want to understand if rating is collinear and calculate its VIF - this is what one does: evaluate a model in which we regress the other factors on rating    summary(lm(rating~age+limit,data=credit)), which yields Call:lm(formula = rating ~ age + limit, data = credit)Residuals:   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max -31.82  -8.62  -1.30   8.61  30.43 Coefficients:            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    (Intercept) 3.73e+01   2.33e+00   16.02   <2e-16 ***age         2.35e-02   3.57e-02    0.66     0.51    limit       6.68e-02   2.67e-04  250.42   <2e-16 ***---Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1Residual standard error: 12.2 on 397 degrees of freedomMultiple R-squared:  0.994,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.994 F-statistic: 3.17e+04 on 2 and 397 DF,  p-value: <2e-16Now we have the R squared for this model, 0.994 and plugging that into the formula provided 1/(1+R2) we get 161 as indicated (or as obtained if we use vif in package car) (note you need to use the entire digits to get 161, one can access the value usingsummary(lm(rating~age+limit,data=credit))$r.squared)Now this makes perfect sense to me - we basically measured how much of the variation in rating we can explain by the other variables and the answer is 99.4%.In fact if you do the model for rating regressed on limit you get the 99.4% as wellNow that I understand this, I do not need to ever again do it - I am happy calling vif or other function to automate this in RI hope this helps others"	0	0	0	4	5	3.5	Humanities	52e717c12d0ca06c9600002b	HumanitiesScience/StatLearning/Winter2014	162D724973AE2B89BA8D72C97D331DD5	1/28/2014 2:36	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	2	None	351

"Staff: Great discussion and I agree with your observations and explanations above.  I too have this problem when hiking. As stated above:1) It is worse with a backpack (impaired venous return)2) It is worse in the heat (peripheral vasodilation leading to leakage into interstitial spaces)3) It is worse when my arms are still and hanging (no muscle pump action).  When you contract your muscles they push on the veins. The veins have one-way valves that then force the blood back to the heart. No contraction = no muscle pump = more blood pooling. The poles help because of muscle pump and less gravity to overcome the full length of your arms (just hooking your fingers in the straps of your backpack to bend your arms up will help too)4) It happens more the longer I am hiking in a particular day and the more tired I am (less venous tone). Over time, you lose the ability to constrict down vessels to the non-active tissue due to fatigue of the vessels. That will also increase blood pooling to those areas.Isn't it fun to think about why these things happen?  Next time you are hiking you can hold up your hand to your bud and explain. Sweet!"	1	0	0	4	3	2	Humanities	52e732f28e1ef8b3ba000078	HumanitiesSciences/EP101/Environmental_Physiology	261F8F6E8B46A29D1D12E5CB0E262DD9	1/28/2014 4:32	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	2	52dda00be37bb299e1000018	239

"In one case you're looking at the probability of the confidence interval encompassing a parameter. In the other you're looking at the probability of a parameter falling within a confidence interval. It's a matter of perspective.When we evaluate study results we're essentially asking if the results we see are likely to have occurred by chance, and the confidence interval defines the range of values we would expect by chance. As **alhf** writes below, the confidence interval is not about trying to predict the outcome.I hope that helps."	0	0	1	4	4	2.5	Humanities	52e748da2d0ca01ed0000047	HumanitiesScience/StatLearning/Winter2014	32BB1EECE714ACCCB3EE1610283F0EE6	1/28/2014 6:06	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	52e55be09b16c7d52600004d	1553

"The **attach()** command in R makes it very easy to specify objects in your code. Be careful, though, because it is possible to attach two dataframes that contain the same variable name. If you do this, you may end up using the wrong data in your analysis.There is a **detach()** command that removes an attached dataframe. Make it your friend if you choose to use attach().I've chosen not to use attach(). Typing *data$var* is a little more work, but I don't have to keep track of what I've attached and I feel it makes my code easier to read when I'm debugging or coming back to something later. You'll figure out what works best for you. "Another gotcha using `attach()` is that it places a **copy** of the object on to the search path. If you alter the original object, those changes are not reflected in the copy on the search path.If you are working at the command line, i.e. not programming in a function, then consider `with()` & `transform()` as alternatives to littering your code with `foo$bar`.For example:    set.seed(1)    df <- data.frame(A = rnorm(10, mean = 4), B = rnorm(10, mean = -3))    with(df, mean(A)) ## mean of A, same as mean(df$A)If you want to alter a variable in a data frame, use `transform()`, e.f.    df <- transform(df, A = sqrt(A), C = B^2)    head(df)        R> head(df)          A      B      C    1 1.837 -1.488  2.215    2 2.045 -2.610  6.813    3 1.779 -3.621 13.113    4 2.365 -5.215 27.193    5 2.081 -1.875  3.516    6 1.783 -3.045  9.272Also, use the formula interface to functions where they exist, i.e.    plot(A ~ B, data = df)is nicer than    plot(df$B, df$A)etc."	0	0	0	4	3	3	Humanities	52e7e23394cae3348900002f	HumanitiesScience/StatLearning/Winter2014	5C2B9BEC352015DFB3ED4C4FD6D74BE1	1/28/2014 17:00	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	5	52e7518f4c0c9bd8f300001b	1077

"I think it's important to think about the context in which women are giving birth when thinking about the safety of medicalized versus home-based practices.  First, among many home birth midwives in the US at least, I know that prenatal care and nutritional support are key, as well as screening for risks such as gestational diabetes and pregnancy induced high blood pressure throughout pregnancy.  Ideally, homebirth would be part of a comprehensive health care system that included collaborations among midwives, doctors, and other health care providers.  This is not yet a reality in the US.  A safe home birth, though, has many pre-requisites that among many (though not all) North Americans are givens.  For example, you can't have a safe home birth if you don't have access to clean water, or if you didn't get enough food, or enough of the right kinds of food, throughout your pregnancy.  So although in the US there is a growing body of research supporting the safety of homebirths, with credentialed professionals, and with the assumption that women's basic needs are met and that they are being screened for risk from the time they inquire about starting care with a midwife up till the time they give birth. "The set.seed function is used so that so that random numbers generated following set.seed will be the same. It is often used in examples in a text book to ensure that the example in the text is reproducible. For example: x= rnorm (50) , y=x+ rnorm (50 , mean =50 , sd =.1) , cor (x,y) will return different values for cor(x,y) depending on the random numbers generated. However set.seed(1303) , x= rnorm (50) , y=x+ rnorm (50 , mean =50 , sd =.1) , cor (x,y)will generate the same result for cor(x,y)Any integer can be used as the argument for set.seed."	0	0	1	4	3	2.5	Humanities	52e821774c0c9bc9b6000045	HumanitiesScience/StatLearning/Winter2014	EF8F0124E4F0DCB05BDB6457E1D05015	1/28/2014 21:30	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	52e2c98a09b4e96cb300000a	379

Could I then examine those 100 confidence intervals> looking at which single value is in nearly all of those> intervals, and then declare that value the \true\"" value?There is no guarantee that ANY of the confidence intervalswill \""capture\"" the true value.  You'd *expect* 95% of themto contain the true value, but it would be *possible* foryou to be very unlucky and get 100 data sets where *none*of the confidence intervals contained the true value.Also, you'd probably find that there was no *single* valuein nearly all intervals, but rather a *range* of values thatwere in nearly all intervals.  This range would be narrowerthan each of the individual confidence intervals.  You could*sort of* think of this \""range of overlap\"" as being anarrower confidence interval.  (And \""narrower\"" is a goodthing for a confidence interval).In practice, if you had 100 data sets each with 20 cointosses, you would put them all together to make a singledata set with 2000 coin tosses and construct a confidenceinterval from that.  The standard error of the big data setwould be less than that of a single sample.  Thiscorresponds to the everyday intuition that \""the average ismore precise if you average a larger number ofobservations\"".So you'd get a narrower confidence intervalwhen you constructed it from the big set (all the data)"""	0	1	1	4	4.5	5	Humanities	52e8256d80ed51ae64000019	HumanitiesScience/StatLearning/Winter2014	5905DB78313C20260A8B5B4B33C40AAE	1/28/2014 21:47	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	2	52e55be09b16c7d52600004d	1553

"I think the wording of the question is a little twisted around from the normal usage.  Typically the null hypothesis would be that B1 = 0, in which case: - rejecting the null hypothesis would require a confidence interval that does not contain 0 and - NOT rejecting the null hypothesis would require a confidence interval that does contain 0But since in this particular question, the null hypothesis takes the form of B1 = b: - rejecting the null hypothesis would require a confidence interval that does not contain b and - NOT rejecting the null hypothesis would require a confidence interval that does contain bIt's the latter case we're concerned with here, so we need a confidence interval that does contain b.  Since b = 0.5, SE = 0.2, and CI = b +/- 2*SE, the confidence interval is [0.1, 0.9].  So the \largest value of b for which we would NOT reject the null hypothesis that B1 = b\"" is 0.9, the top end of that CI.Hope this helps...Thanks,<nameRedac_<anon_screen_name_redacted>>"""	0	0	0	4	4.5	3.5	Humanities	52e8639380ed51e9ee000028	HumanitiesScience/StatLearning/Winter2014	640AA4F9509B3C3FB82563A5D71FA170	1/29/2014 2:12	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	8	52e8484d80ed5107e3000028	1218
