"The purpose of rent control, as I understand it, are to assure that those with the lowest level of income have rental housing available to them at a price they can afford when there is a shortage in the market. When there is a shortage of housing, people selecting the least expensive options will pay whatever they are able to, as the alternative is to be homeless (low demand elasticity). "Hey bliutwo,This question requires you to play around a bit to find the efficient outcome. Notice that the first question required you to see if the \2 and 2\"" production combination was Pareto Efficient...First off, the efficient outcome is the combination of production at Firm A and Firm B such that neither firm can be made better off without making the other worse off.  A couple of different options:**Scenario 1:** Firm A produces 2 and Firm B produces 2. We note that: 1. Firm A's profit = -2 2. Firm B's profit = -3 3. Total profit = -5 4. Total cost is 17.**Scenario 2:** Firm A produces 1 and Firm B produces 3. We note that: 1. Firm A's profit = 0  2. Firm B's profit = -2 3. Total profit = -2 4. Total cost = 20. Notice that both Firm A and Firm B's profits improve under this scenario. Scenario 1 was not Pareto Efficient.**Scenario 3:** Firm A produces 3 and Firm B produces 1. We note that: 1. Firm A's Profit = 1 2. Firm B's Profit = -2 3. Total profit is -1  4. ***Total Cost is 16*** (Look at the total cost for each firm at their respective level of production to derive this number)Now notice that under this scenario Firm A's position improves while Firm B's position remains unchanged, i.e. Firm B is not made worse off by Firm A's gain. Therefore Scenario 2 was not Pareto Efficient!If you look at the other possible production combinations it should become quickly apparent that Scenario 3 is that outcome where neither firm can be made better off without making the other firm worse off if the production combination changes. The Total Cost, i.e. the combined total costs for Firm A and Firm B under the efficient outcome (Scenario 3) is 16.Cheers,Nick"""	0	0	1	4	3	2.5	Humanities	53b48fb1482e492224000090	HumanitiesSciences/Econ1V/Summer2014	6B943017712380B5B3AE63EDE404CFD5	7/2/2014 23:03	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	53b47d3695bec26d9c00008b	19

"I think the resolution is that consumers have a wide variety of options of products on which to spend their money.For example, say I'm a consumer who has 10 dollars to spend.There is a product X that costs 4 dollars / unit has a marginal benefit of 5 dollars for 1 unit purchased and a marginal benefit of 3 dollars for 2 units purchased.If, as a consumer with a 10 dollar budget, product X is the only product available for me to purchase in the market, I will maximize my utility (total marginal benefit) by purchasing two of product X for a total utility of 8 dollars.However, let's introduce a product Y that costs 4 dollars / unit and has a marginal benefit of 4 dollars for 1 unit purchased and a marginal benefit of 2 dollars for 2 units purchased.Now, as a consumer, I can maximize my utility (total marginal benefit) by purchasing 1 unit of product X and 1 unit of product Y for a total utility of 9 dollars.If either product X or product Y exists in isolation, my maximum utility is achieved by purchasing two units of the product. However, if both of these products exist together in the market -- a good model of the real world -- then I will purchase one of each.In general, a purchase can be thought of as a transaction of value, and consumers will optimize utility (total marginal benefit) among many product options by only making positive or break even value transactions.For example, let product Z cost 4.50 dollars / unit and have a marginal benefit of 5 dollars for 1 unit purchased and 3 dollars for 2 units purchased.Purchasing 1 unit of product Z is a value transaction of - 4.50 dollars of monetary value and + 5 dollars of marginal benefit value for a total value of + 0.50 dollars. It is in a consumer's best interest to make this positive value transaction.However, purchasing 2 units of product Z is a value transaction of - 9 dollars of monetary value and + 8 dollars of marginal benefit value for a total value of - 1 dollars. A consumer will avoid this negative value transaction in a market with many options in favor of other value transactions that are positive or break even in total value payoff."	1	0	0	4	3.5	2.5	Humanities	53b582ce90ef61231400005a	HumanitiesSciences/Econ-1/Summer2014	630B20D559898A85CFDE0AEA50F4F7B8	7/3/2014 16:20	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	1	53b172c36216cf1768000049	137

"Hi, I got all those wrong as well, but now I understand why.Shifts in demand occur when something besides a change in price changes the quantity of a good that people are willing to buy. Shifts in supply occur when something besides a change in price changes the quantity of a good that people are willing to sell.Although it may seem like that as the price increases, you have more \demand\"", in reality, the demand has not shifted at all. This seems a bit counterintuitive. Let me repeat. The demand has not increased for bicycles nor has it increased. The quantity supplied however, changes in response to changes in price.i.e. as the price increases, the quantity supplied increases. The demand does not change. As the price decreases, the quantity supplied decreases.Another way of looking at it is the equilibrium supply and demand model. As we go up along the demand curve as the price increases, so too does our supply increase. As we go down along the demand curve as the price decreases, so too does supply respond in turn. What happens if we change the demand or change the supply. Well, if we translate our demand curve to the right, then the equilibrium price will increase which results in a net increase for the price of the bicycles. If the amount of bicycles supplied decreases, the supply curve is translated to the left. That in turn raises the equilibrium price which also in turn raises the price. It's very subtle, but it has a lot of implications. Price increase and quantity supplied means movement along the demand curve. Alternatively, you can think about if price decreases, then the amount supplied decreases. Market equilibrium, however will gravitate towards when the amount demanded equals the amount supplied. Demand increases shifts the equilibrium price up (think translation of the demand curve), and if supply is kept the same, raises prices. If the supply of bicycles increases (think again translation of the supply curve), and the demand is kept constant, the equilibrium price decreases, and price decreases. I feel as if Professor Taylor could have stressed this fact in the preceding video before the quiz; however, the video with market equilibrium after the quiz was illuminating and really brought all these concepts together."""	1	0	0	3	4.5	4.5	Humanities	53b7ad3499cc9d67ef000011	HumanitiesSciences/Econ-1/Summer2014	575A53CEEF968B8AB9B7B70A76C9C0E8	7/5/2014 7:45	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	1	53b3d652482e492224000038	111

"The supply of housing in SF is less than the market equilibrium, as more housing is demanded than is available. The biggest problem is that producers/sellers of housing have built mostly higher priced homes that are only in the price range of high income people but too high for medium- and low-income people. In a normal market, the invisible hand would have this dictate that the equilibrium price be a higher price; however, with rent control in place there is essentially a price ceiling in place to make housing more affordable to low- and medium-income buyers.  Therefore, for the market, the marginal benefit to consumers is not equal to the marginal cost for sellers. Sellers of higher priced condos will not be able to sell them for the appropriate marginal cost due to the price ceiling, meaning that there is a deadweight loss as the gain for buyers harms sellers. This housing market is inefficient since MB does not equal MC, and MC for each producer is not the same because sellers that have spent more on building a condo may be forced to rent it at the same price as sellers that have spent less if both are selling the respective properties at the ceiling price. This market can't be efficient, unless builders build more low-cost housing that is affordable to the medium- and lower-income buyers. But, due to not enough land being available and no shortage of buyers willing to pay high prices, there is little incentive for sellers to build low-cost homes."	1	0	0	4	3.5	2.5	Humanities	53b82e28471e2fa54100001e	HumanitiesSciences/Econ1V/Summer2014	AE58EBCDBF9ECB60B95A4354C7FC943D	7/5/2014 16:56	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	7

"\Is there a way to keep the price of housing low while keeping the market efficient?\""I don't know.  But here are my responses to the questions above:Q:  Is the market for housing in San Francisco Pareto efficient?  What about deadweight loss?  A:  The current housing market in San Francisco is not Pareto efficient.  One condition that must be met if a market is to be Pareto efficient is this:  the marginal benefit, or demand curve, must intersect the marginal cost, or supply curve, at a single point.   Enforcing a price ceiling on housing rentals stymies the convergence of supply and demand to a single point of intersection, where MB = MC, by stripping the market’s suppliers of the incentive to produce more units until all excess demand is exhausted.  A price ceiling set lower than market equilibrium curbs the quantity (and possibly the quality) of rental units supplied to the market as suppliers forego more production despite the presence of excess demand (MB > MC).  When a market suffers this ‘lost production’ despite excess demand, producer and consumer surpluses are not maximized as they should be to achieve Pareto efficiency.  The lost production acts as deadweight on the economy and may render the rent control policy self-defeating from the start.Q:  Is there a way to keep the price of housing low while keeping the market efficient? Why or why not? A: Perhaps a way to keep the price of housing low is to consider ways of encouraging suppliers to produce (smaller) higher margin housing units for the “affordable” market?"""	1	0	0	4	3.5	3	Humanities	53b8602899cc9de49b00002b	HumanitiesSciences/Econ-1/Summer2014	F0729A1B5D6E302196F9850376D17F7D	7/5/2014 20:29	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	53b85b4499cc9d67ef000034	23

"I don't think you should think of it in terms of how many unit a consumer is purchasing and then averaging out the price per unit.  For example, I don't have a car and when I go to the dealer to purchase my first car, I am willing to price that first car a little higher. "Marginal cost increases due to the increasing fixed costs. With more being produced, investment is necessary for new equipment, facilities, and workers. Further, overall marginal productivity decreases with more production. To make a profit, the producer's selling price must exceed marginal cost. Product maximization aims to achieve the highest possible level of profits, so a firm will continue production until marginal revenue will become equal to marginal cost. "To answer the opening questions first:1. Marginal cost increases as more is produced because of the diminishing returns of labor - the marginal product of labor decreases as more is produced.  Your costs for each subsequent item produced increases at a faster rate the more you produce.2. Profit maximization means that firms will try to maximize revenue while minimizing costs (since profit is revenue minus costs).  For a given market price, this means they want to produce as much as possible to sell while keeping cost as low as possible.  The marginal cost is the amount that it costs to produce one additional unit of an item.  If this cost is more than the firm can sell that item for, it will not be following the profit maximization mantra of maximizing revenue while minimizing costs.  Costs will have exceeded potential revenue.3. In a competitive market, firms or producers are not setting the price.  As such, they have to produce based on the market price, so the only way for them to maximize profits would be to make sure that marginal costs do not exceed the price (their potential revenue).  In a non-competitive market or one where producers could set the price, they could simply charge over the marginal cost for a given production quantity, ensuring that their revenue exceeds their costs.  This would allow for theoretically limitless profit.The oil market appears to be not perfectly competitive from the little information that was contained in the article. So from that standpoint, the market does seem competitive.I understand that in a competitive market, producers do not set the price.  But the idea that they cannot affect the market price at all seems like an oversimplification. "The market for housing in San Francisco is NOT efficient in pareto standards.  In this situation, it is not impossible to make one person better off without hurting another person.  The enforcement of rent control places a price ceiling on the market to make housing more affordable to people who can’t typically afford more expensive housing.  This means that the marginal benefit to consumers is not equal to the marginal cost for producers (the benefit of the last unit produced is not equal to the cost of that unit), therefore, creating an inefficient market.  Additionally, the producers of more expensive housing will not be able to sell their housing at appropriate prices, resulting in a deadweight loss.  This is lost surplus for the suppliers as the buyers are benefitted.  There is not an easy way to keep prices low in an efficient market, because there will always be plenty of people willing to pay the ceiling price and the producers that produce at these prices will have little incentive to lower their quality of production."	1	0	0	4	3.5	2.5	Humanities	53bb719eac6b323a56000008	HumanitiesSciences/Econ1V/Summer2014	DA4C5A630087639446F3FA563E6DD7DB	7/8/2014 4:20	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	6

"This is a great question. It's a little outside the scope of the class but no worries. There really isn't a single theory for oligopolies however the most frequently discussed is the kinked-demand curve. The basic idea is that oligopolies would compete in the market via differentiated products (again, not something we've covered). You could think of this as the difference between Chevron's Techron gas and Shell's V-Power (\Premium\"") gas. Essentially the same product, i.e. gasoline, but differentiated slightly.Firms theoretically face multiple demand curves in the market. Let's take an example where there are only two firms. Theory models the demand curves for each product with slightly different slopes and intersecting at some unique point. Reducing the price below this intersection will move consumers from one demand curve to another! (I'd suggest drawing this out)  Think about this a bit... which demand curve are consumers on over the entire range of prices?From the firms' perspectives, the demand curve they face is kinked, i.e. kinked at the point of intersection. It makes sense that consumers would take a lower price for only slightly differentiated products, right?In addition, the Marginal Revenue curve will have a discontinuity, aka a \""jump\"" (again, drawing this out will help). Mathematically, the first derivative at the point of the kink in the demand curve is undefined, thus the jump discontinuity in the marginal revenue curve. (you'll play with this more in Econ 51). As for MC and ATC:Remember the firm's supply curve is simply it's MC curve. At this point in the course we're trying to get you comfortable thinking about the supply curve as the MC curve. It (and the ATC) are going to look similar to the curves faced by firms in competitive markets. Remember, these firms are not natural monopolies... and so they do not have declining ATCs over the entire range of their production.Hope that helps and doesn't cloud the issue too much. There's plenty of info on the web if you're interested in going deeper on this.Nick"""	0	0	1	4	2.5	3.5	Humanities	53bc91dbac6b32edda000070	HumanitiesSciences/Econ1V/Summer2014	6B943017712380B5B3AE63EDE404CFD5	7/9/2014 0:50	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	53bbf32dac6b32195300001e	10

"The reason why players leave early is a) to maximize their total career earning potential (players only will be able to play basketball for a finite number of years, and, for the top players, the NBA has maximum salary restrictions that limit the amount of additional salary a player can earn each year, so a player whose first contract is at age 18 can make far more money over the course of his career than one who starts at age 22) and b) the majority of top prospects who don't enter the draft see their draft stock drop in subsequent years, which means they'll earn less money from their first contracts.The NBA used to allow players to jump straight from high school to the NBA, and it was a huge problem because it was too difficult for the NBA to evaluate players who hadn't yet played in college. As a result, the NBA draft became a crapshoot, where teams were investing top picks in unproven high school players that then took years to develop (and many never did). Requiring high school stars to play at least one year of school made drafting much easier, and decreased the amount of resources NBA teams now need to devote towards developing young players.Requiring players to spend 4 years in college has significant drawbacks as well. The biggest is the simple fact that top college stars are often ready to play in the NBA at age 19, and requiring them to stay an extra three years in college is lost revenue (i.e. \opportunity cost\"") for the league.  One clear example: Derrick Rose won the NBA MVP Award in what would've been his senior year in college.  More stars in the league equals a better product for consumers.  Also, requiring players to stay 4 years might lead some top high school players to play in Europe rather than playing in college, which is bad for the league for a number of reasons, including the potential that they will sign long-term contracts in Europe and either not come to the NBA or require NBA teams to buy out their contracts.The question asks to make the case for eliminating the restriction on college or requiring 4 years -- but both of those are bad options. What the NBA has recently been considering (and reportedly tried to push for in the 2011 Collective Bargaining Agreement) is a 2-year college requirement.I think a 2-year requirement makes a lot of sense. It gives the NBA one additional year to observe and evaluate prospects, and it reduces the resources the league must devote to developing young players. An example would be melon: you and me, we are selling melon in a market at a certain price; at a moment, for any reason, more and more people are coming and want(!) to buy melons; that much that we see that we will run out of our stock; so in that moment we raise our price (or organise an auction - anticipating the same). The supply/demand diagram (or 'curve') does not talk about what I've described until now. But if we raised our price too high and lots of people decide to buy apples... That is the topic of the next lessons.] The supply-curve describes our thought at the moment when we see the sudden crowed approaching our stand: \Oh, we gonna raise the price - and we need more melons to sell!\"".Now, let's come back to our lesson. These 2 diagrams are models, and as they are, actually, they are very simple ones - for beginners as we are :-) They are not going to explain real situations in details. "For heavy users of tech, cloud storage is increasingly becoming a necessity for which they will pay a considerable price. However, many casual phone and tablet users have no need for cloud storage at high prices--the marginal benefit of even 1 GB of cloud storage simply isn't very high for them. Of course, these users would gravitate toward Google's free offering. Now, however, Google is making a play for slightly heavier users--people who could use more than 15GB but wouldn't pay much for it. Now, prices are going to be in line with marginal benefit for a larger number of consumers--increasing the quantity demanded. "\Our Peter Orszag Problem\"" is an example of the concept of government failure in which self-interested behavior on the part of government employees can lead to actions and decisions that bring benefits to them and work against the interest of the public. More specifically, the article demonstrates two concepts pointed out in the discussion of government failure. One is the model of public choice in which those in government take actions that maximize their own well-being and the other is regulatory capture in which a regulator is likely to come from the very industry he or she is regulating, then administers the agency in a manner favorable to the industry, and finally leaves the agency for position with the very industry that was regulated.Even after leaving government service, the former regulator can still affect government policy. Perhaps the successor to the position was a subordinate who owes the job to her or his former superior and is likely to keep in contact now that the former regulator is in private industry. Even if the successor is not a former subordinate, the former regulator shaped policy under some executive such as a state governor or the President of the United States. The bonds of a working relationship with the executive are not likely to be completely broken, so the former regulator can contact her or his former superior to influence the policy choice for the industry.Preventing potential conflicts of interest has been difficult. A presidential order prohibiting taking a job with a firm that was regulated by the individual for a period of time has not worked. Appointing a regulator from outside the industry being regulated may result in a lack of knowledge about the industry to effectively regulate it. One possible alternative may be to use legislative oversight to approve changes in regulatory policy as a foil to regulatory capture and industry influence. There is no guarantee, however, that legislators will not be influenced directly by the industries being regulated beyond being voted out of office by the electorate for approving policy changes against the public interest."""	1	0	0	4	4	3	Humanities	53c913fcd31cd46910000022	HumanitiesSciences/Econ-1/Summer2014	85614C5FA0854B744DF7418B8D83925C	7/18/2014 12:33	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	20

"The 1996 law attempted to increase the incentive to work through welfare reform. "Google took a price-cut strategy to tackle the market head-on. A customer has to pay 2 dollaars for 100GB storage, and if there is no price cut, he or she should spend 20 dollars to possess 1TB, but now it costs only $10. The strategy is consistent with the demand curve and the diminishing marginal benefit. The demand curve slopes downward because of declining marginal benefit, in this case, customers have a declining willingness to pay for more storage. "The thing is, \education\"" isn't one single thing. It can be split up into \""elementary education,\"" \""secondary education,\"" and \""college education.\"" And in fact, even \""college education\"" can be split into the separate *products*, if you can call it that, of \""public college education,\"" \""Ivy League education,\"" etc. With that in mind, let's see which of these are public goods.First off, elementary and secondary education are public goods. They are state-funded, and barring the cases of the severely understaffed schools in impoverished areas, they are non-rival and non-excludable (although the students do have the option to drop out after a certain point).As for college education, this is where it gets tricky. A college education is definitely excludable when the product being sold is \""college education at Harvard,\"" but not so much when it is \""college education at your local community college.\"" It is non-rival if the product is \""college education from online classes,\"" but it is rival if the product is \""college education at ________ exclusive university\"" (although you could argue that relative to the people already in the university, it is non-rival because attending lectures is free).One unifying factor, though, is that education causes positive externalities. An informed populace has higher wealth, satisfaction, and quality of life. Even those who do not have a higher education benefit from economic increases caused by those who do. The government is therefore subsidizing college education for many incoming college students. Of course, this comes with downsides too: because more students are being subsidized, colleges raise tuition costs, contributing to the rampant problem of student debt. This is, in fact, a negative externality of subsidies given to only certain students. The ones who aren't subsidized have to face a higher cost."""	1	0	0	4	4	2.5	Humanities	53cb4b3a1e43f351e9000049	HumanitiesSciences/Econ-1/Summer2014	EC842275D957A31A5DB985986FC83CF2	7/20/2014 4:53	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	2	None	35

"Can anyone explain how we know that the firms' profits will be reduced?Presumably we are in a competitive market initially, so profits are zero and production is at the market equilibrium. Now the government introduces the wage cap. This causes a movement along the labour supply curve - the price of labour has been set, so the quantity supplied will drop accordingly. Firms demand more labour than is available, so there is a deficit of labour, but the cap prevents them from raising wages in response. As the quantity of labour is reduced, the quantity of goods produced is reduced. This reduces the marginal cost of production (diminishing returns on labour mean it's more efficient to produce smaller amounts).At this lower quantity of production, demand is higher than supply, so the price is higher than the marginal cost of producing the goods. This leads to a deadweight loss in the market, but also a profit for the firms. So, lower quantity, higher price, lower marginal costs. Unless we know the elasticities of supply and demand, for both labour and the good(s) being produced, we don't know the relative sizes of these effects. So how can we say whether profits will be higher or lower?"	1	0	0	4	5	4.5	Humanities	53cbf642e0c1132909000025	HumanitiesSciences/Econ-1/Summer2014	A8888E58DCFE447711908830B8BF93D3	7/20/2014 17:02	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	1	None	31

"The paper written by the two economists argues the point of how the Department of Justice erred far better than I could.  From what I gather, the antitrust regulations of the Sherman Act and other legislation define price fixing in a necessarily narrow and limited fashion.  If it did not, conceivably any action by a group of firms could be construed as price fixing.  For example, if a shortage of a given material critical to production in a given industry drove all firms in that industry to raise their prices, this could be called \price fixing\"" in that the all firms seemingly \""conspired\"" to raise their prices.Fortunately, our country's antitrust legislation does not leave this loophole open.  Price fixing is defined specifically as \""horizontal\"" collusion between firms in an industry to set the price at a level that would not otherwise be in the independent firms' interests.  We can think of the game theory example here for a duopoly, where if each firm were to act independently of the other, both would elect to \""cheat\"" or lower their prices in order to sell more product.  Independent of each other, this is how they would behave, for it is in the best interest of each firm to do so.  Collusion and price-fixing occurs when both firms agree to set the price higher and sell less, separate from the independent benefit each would see from selling more at a lower price.As the amici curiae paper argues, Apple's actions do not fall into this narrow definition, and thus cannot be rightly considered \""price fixing.\""  This was not \""horizontal\"" collusion - Apple did not conspire with Amazon and agree to raise prices.  It is unlikely that Amazon would have even entered into such an agreement, since they already owned the majority of the market share and would have seen Apple only as a potential competitor that they would like to keep out of the market if they could.  Instead, Apple had to find a roundabout way to gain entry into the market at all - going directly to the publishers, who were already unhappy with the losses in their profits due to the rise of ebooks and Amazon's ability to undercut competitive prices.  Apple's deal with the publishers is thus not \""horizontal\"" in nature.Furthermore, Apple's actions are entirely in its own interests independent of any collusion or price-fixing.  It would benefit Apple to enter the ebook industry, regardless of Apple's ability to \""fix\"" the price of said products, so long as it could reasonably expect to profit in the l"""	1	0	0	4	3.5	3	Humanities	53cc8191ed1b8a864f00002f	HumanitiesSciences/Econ-1/Summer2014	DFBB4607E47EF3C098B1F6B28D14E4B1	7/21/2014 2:57	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	20

"In theory, I believe education should be a public good, but in our current school systems it is not. There is a massive quality gap in education that is a result of public versus private funding, quality of the school district, presence of charter schools, and institutional practices. Because the quality of education is not the same across the nation, it cannot be deemed a public good in the same way that national defense can. Education is rivalrous and excludable. It is excludable because certain social injustices prevent certain types of students from accessing education in the same ways that other students are able to. For example, individuals coming from various socio-economic statuses may have varying resources to buy school supplies, receive help on homework, receive proper nutrition for development, etc. As compared to national defense where anyone receives protection regardless of race, class, or gender, education does not provide the same blanket coverage. Additionally, education is rivalrous. I would consider education to be a limited resource, especially higher education such as college. There are a limited number of spots for attendance and a limited number of scholarships to enable students to attend college. For this reason, education is rivalrous because one student's access prevents another student from accessing it. In a perfect world, education would be a public good provided with equal quality to all people but that is not the current state of affairs in the United States education system."	1	0	0	4	4	2.5	Humanities	53cd9c5368565ac5ec000030	HumanitiesSciences/Econ1V/Summer2014	779603F47E9E5D4CD487BD2383886007	7/21/2014 23:03	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	1

"I'm going to disagree with many of the other posts here and argue that while traditional elementary education may be *delivered* like a public good in countries like the US, it is fundamentally no different from private postsecondary education (not a public good).**Not non-rival:** A single teacher can only teach a finite number of students, and the quality of education is generally accepted as higher in smaller classes. Adding another child to a classroom either displaces another child or decreases the quality of education for the rest of the class.**Not non-excludable:** Barring someone access to education is as simple as restricting their physical access to a school. Looking at global access to education issues (particularily among girls and young women) makes this painfully clear.Given that even traditional elementary level education can be shown to be neither non-rival nor non-excludable, I  would contend that it is not a public good, at any level (unfortunately). However, advances in technology (infinite duplicability and access to information via the internet, and MOOCs like this one) are in the process of changing that.However, I would agree that education has significant positive externalities, in particular at the lowest levels (elementary, etc). The benefits of a literate population, for example, are far greater than the sum of private benefits to literate individuals. In my view it's these major positive externalities that justify delivering elementary education publicly (ie completely subsidized)."	1	0	0	4	3.5	3	Humanities	53cdbae068565a98a000003d	HumanitiesSciences/Econ-1/Summer2014	C67B83B5BD60A466EDC662C1855625BE	7/22/2014 1:14	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	0	None	37

Anyone who knows about the housing market knows that the \""price\"" of housing is not the actual price of the house itself, but rather it is the mortgage rate. At high mortgage rates, a home buyer may be limited in terms of the homes that are available and these homes may not be desirable because they don't fit a purchaser's needs. As mortgage rates go down, a home buyer is able to afford a more expensive home. This is a condition similar to what was discussed in the article; that the lower mortgage rates drove the housing price-to-income ratio from 3:1 to 5:1. Thus far financial institutions have been rather reluctant to take advantage of this largess perhaps because they do not want their shareholders or financial regulators to think they are once again being irresponsible lenders. At some point, however, this risk aversion will subside as investors demand higher returns for the cash they have sunk into these institutions.So financial institutions eventually will make mortgages available to home buyers at current interest rates and home buyers will look for and purchase homes that meet their projected mortgage payments, even if they are more expensive. This means that the housing price-to-income ratio will increase just as it did before the financial crisis. "It's significant for central planning ideologies. It is essentially an attempt at very broad aggregation over diverse things so as to pretend we can make sense of large scale economic trends, although very little forecasting ability has ever been demonstrated.Is Macroeconomics Really Economics?By Robert Higgs	The world probably would have been much better off had macroeconomics never been devised. Although I have in mind Keynesian macroeconomics above all, I include other types of macro models as well. I even include, somewhat reluctantly, the whole quantity theory approach descended from David Hume to the Friedmanites, now known as monetarism.One of monetarism’s aspects that bothered me long before I became an Austrian (of sorts) is its oversimplification of aggregate economic activity. Resting their analysis on (a more or less elaborated version of) the Fisherian equation of exchange, monetarists maintain that changes in nominal aggregate demand (hence movements in either real output or the price level) occur in response to changes in the money stock (absent offsetting changes in the demand for money). To me this idea seemed to be a claim that the money-stock tail can and does wag the aggregate economic dog; that, more specifically, in a situation of sub-capacity real output (“recession” or “depression”), increases in money stock—and only such increases—drive increases in real output and employment.Because I believed, and still believe, that changes in aggregate output and employment may occur also as a result of changes in other variables (e.g., investors’ perceptions of the future security of their private property rights [\regime uncertainty\""]), monetarism always seemed to me to claim an implausibly high degree of explanatory power, some of which might be concealed by spurious empirical correlations between money and total output à la Friedman and Schwartz.In short, among its many other deficiencies, as spelled out by Mises and his followers, monetarism’s most fundamental flaw is identical to the most fundamental flaw of Keynesian, Post-Keynesian, New Classical, and other theories advanced by macroeconomists during the past seventy or eighty years: not only does the theory leave out critical variables, but it is too simple, being expressed in huge, all-encompassing aggregates that conceal the real economic action taking place within the economic order.-------------------\""Alchian didn’t deny there were aggregate economic phenomena, only """	1	0	0	4	3.5	3.5	Humanities	53cef31dcaaf0ea0d1000054	HumanitiesSciences/Econ-1/Summer2014	48337FB2A4B80C38E79790679991D8DE	7/22/2014 23:26	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	53ca87c01e43f351e9000011	38

"It is very interesting to see that there are such conflicting data with regard to the employment effects of the minimum wage.  The supply and demand model for competitive markets would typically predict that a minimum wage would ALWAYS reduce employment.  However, there are several exceptions that I can think of, where perhaps a minimum wage carefully implemented would not have an overall negative effect on employment, as the article suggests.As Professor Taylor discussed in the video, a steep demand curve for labor would mean that a minimum wage would have very little effect on employment.  There are any number of factors that could lead to such a demand curve.  As the article alludes to, continuing technological advancements leading to greater workplace efficiency and ultimately greater productivity could offset the increase to production costs that come with a higher minimum wage.  Thus demand would keep pace with a rising wage, since firms would still be trying to maximize profits under the competitive paradigm, just with greater productive capacity as a result of technological advances.Additionally, the effects of minimum wage on employment depend on the segment of the labor population.  The competitive model does not predict reduced employment in labor markets where the market equilibrium wage is already above the minimum wage.  This is the equivalent of a government floor below the equilibrium price, which has no effect on the market, at least according to the supply and demand paradigm.  Thus, a cleverly implemented minimum wage could target specifically those low-income, unskilled labor segments that most need it at a time when overall employment in industry sectors that operate above the minimum wage is on the rise.  This would lead to a situation where overall employment numbers could potentially not be affected.  Theoretically, any decrease in employment in the unskilled segment would be offset by a growth in employment in a different sector.This might account for why some studies show that minimum wage does not affect employment, whereas others do.  It all depends on the segment of the labor market being analyzed and also on the timing - what is going on in the economy as a whole?  Is it growing?  For example, is the tech industry booming, creating a high demand for tech jobs that leads to a growth in tech industry employment with wages well above the minimum?"	1	0	0	4	3.5	3.5	Humanities	53d5d6db5c375d0be9000004	HumanitiesSciences/Econ-1/Summer2014	DFBB4607E47EF3C098B1F6B28D14E4B1	7/28/2014 4:51	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	4	None	32

"Operation Twist was an attempt by the Fed to revive a moribund U.S. housing market by purchasing Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities to bring long-term interest rates down to make mortgage lending affordable again and to support the prices of homes after the housing market was devastated as a result of the Great Recession. "Dr. Taylor, they don't understand capital theory. It's very basic but there seems to be a neglect of the temporal arts in economics.Economist Bob Murphy provides a Robinson Crusoe illustration:A Sushi Model of Capital ConsumptionWithout further ado, let's examine a hypothetical island economy composed of 100 people, where the only consumption good is rolls of sushi.The island starts in an initial equilibrium that is indefinitely sustainable. Every day, 25 people row boats out into the water and use nets to catch fish. Another 25 of the islanders go into the paddies to gather rice. Yet another 25 people take rice and fish (collected during the previous day, of course) and make tantalizing sushi rolls. "Einstein is more modern than Newton. I need special and general relativity to use my GPS! Nash made game theory much more relevant to actual economics. What word should I use?\Although the speed with which Nash obtained these results is surprising, equally surprising and certainly less widely known is that Nash had already completed an important piece of work on bargaining while still an under-graduate at the Carnegie Institute of Technology. This work, a paper for an elective course in international economics, possibly the only formal course in economics he has ever had, was done in complete ignorance of the work of von Neumann and Morgenstern. In short, when he did this work he didn’t know that game theory existed. This result, which is a model of theoretical elegance, posits four reasonable requirements or axioms: (1), that any solution should be invariant under positive linear affine transformations of the utility functions, (2), that the solution should be efficient in the sense of Pareto optimality, (3), that irrelevant alternatives should not change the outcome of the solution, and (4), that bargaining problems with symmetric outcome sets should have symmetric solutions. If these four reasonable conditions are satisfied then there is a unique solution, namely, the outcome that maximizes the product of the players’ utilities. There is evidence in the published form of this paper, [37], that, before it appeared in Econometrica in 1950, he had met von Neumann and Morgenstern. "The thing about GDP is that it measures a very specific thing. Specifically, it measures the total amount of production in a country. Realize that, because the real world isn't perfectly competitive, and because big markets tend towards oligopoly, there is often a surplus of products produced, creating deadweight loss while technically increasing the statistic of GDP. If we define GDP as Y = C + I + G + (X-M), then increased consumption could increase the statistic. This is the intended aim of stimulus spending and low interest rates, which hope to encourage more people to consume. However, the amount that the government spends is also counted into the GDP. Think of WWII. While the average person wasn't so well off, the statistic of GDP went sky high simply because of the high government spending on the war. GDP doesn't measure the theoretical maximum-efficiency scenario; by definition, the government will be less Pareto-efficient than the market in its purchases.Overall, the measure of quality of life can be determined with the Human Development Index (HDI). "You idea of \tailing off\"" is a good way how to explain by logic not only the demand curve, but the supply curve as well. If a business owner or manufacturer sees an opportunity to sell for a higher price, he is incentivised by the price increase to produce and sell as much as possible. But since the resources (employees, premises, etc. factors of production) is limited business owner / manufacturer by the price increase tries to optimise and get the most out of the resources it has. So every time when price increases driven by innovation / efficiency / economy of scale / creativity it figures out how to supply even more at the price. The curve \""tails off\"" when the production resources is close to its end and it is impossible to produce even more units than before because of the production possibility curve."""	1	0	0	4	3.5	2.5	Humanities	53e104d0908ff0f5ab000012	HumanitiesSciences/Econ-1/Summer2014	0C347734B906ACBE99531B97F53A1BED	8/5/2014 16:22	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	53b07db16216cf1768000012	45

"From the data presented in the table, it is clear that the proportion of U.S. GDP devoted to consumption has increased over the previous five decades. Moreover, net exports went from a surplus to a deficit during this period, which also reflects Americans growing appetite for goods and services.Because Americans have been consuming more, they necessarily have been saving less of their incomes than before. With less being saved as a proportion of income, it is no wonder that the share of GDP devoted to investment has gone down as well. Thus Americans appear to be more focused on satisfying their wants and desires in the present and have become less concerned about focusing on the future.Canada, on the other hand, has not consumed as much as Americans as a proportion of GDP and in fact consumption to GDP declined slightly in the 50 years period shown in the data. "JamesL, I'm afraid you are confused. I am not talking about sampling. I am asking whether the distribution of heights actually follows a normal distribution. This has nothing to do with sampling. Sampling from a non-normal distribution many times does not convert the distribution into a normal distribution. It may let you construct statistics which are approximately normal, but it does not change the distribution. If you still want to talk about sampling, please make your own thread. I'm talking about the distribution itself.By the way, you seem to be suggesting that all distributions are normal, although it is hard to tell because you may be using the equals sign to mean something other than equality. The space of distributions has infinitely many dimensions. Normal distributions are a very, very special two-dimensional family of distributions. They have many properties not shared with many other typically encountered distributions. For example, they are not skewed. They are continuous and unimodal. They have subexponential tails. So, it is a very strong assertion to say that a distribution (such as that of heights) is normal."	0	0	1	4	3.5	4	Medicine	51b958254983c00e000000d1	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	2F91BA8FE484695ADA8AC8AC45B54891	6/13/2013 5:27	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51b80b26f359c41200000163	275

"It depends on what your objective is. Let's go back to the example in the video, with the age data for 8 people. "Our definitions of common sense may differ. What I usually observe when people refer me to any such thing is just a collection of preconceived notions. "To simplify, use the frequency as number of times a value appears. For example, there are 10 people with a reading of 11, and 9 people with a reading of 12, so when you make the list of readings, you can write it as: 11,11,11,11,11,11,11,11,11,11, 9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9. So in the end you will get a list of 60 numbers, but each number is repeated several times. Then you can use the formulae you know to calculate median, mean, etc."	0	0	1	4	3.5	2.5	Medicine	51bb312f5e980e120000001a	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	7FE1CCA2A420B89B1F1D435A06138CF1	6/14/2013 15:05	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51ba9f909ce05b0e0000007f	103

"I posted this in response to someone else's question, but I see a number of posts asking similar questions, so I posted here as a general aid...Here's how to calculate mean, standard deviation and IQR from a frequency table (referencing homework 1)I do all of this in Excel by the way...Calculate the **mean** using the frequency table given by multiplying each outcome value (11, 12, etc.) by the number of times it occurs (frequency value).  You will end up with six products representing total breaths for each of the six breath outcomes.  For example, the outcome of 11 breaths occurs 10 times.  That's a total breath count of 110 breaths for those 10 people.  Do the same for the other 5 outcome values and their associated frequencies.  Now, add up the six products to get total breaths.  Then, divide that total by 60 to get the average breath count per person. That is your mean.To get the **standard deviation**, calculate the difference between a given breath outcome and your calculated mean (for example: 11 – calculated mean).  Now, square that difference and multiply it by the frequency for that outcome.  The general formula for any given outcome (i) for this first part is: ((outcome(i) – calculated mean)^2) * frequency(i).  In our example: ((11 – calculated mean) ^2) * 10.  That provides the total squared deviations for a single outcome.  Do the same for the other 5 outcome values using your calculated mean and the associated frequency for each outcome.  Now, add up those six total squared deviations to get the grand total squared deviation (GTSD).  Divide that number by n-1 (60-1).  Now, take the square root to get the standard deviation.  So the standard deviation = sqrt(GTSD/(n-1)).The **median** will be the average of two data points in the middle since n is even (60 data points).  So, the median will be the average of points 30 and 31.  What values are at points 30 and 31?  To calculate the IQR, you need the 25th and 75th percentiles.  The **25th percentile** will be the median of the lower 30 data points (1-30).  Again, since the count of the lower 30 points is even, the median will be the average of the two data points in the middle of points 1-30, which will be points 15 & 16.  What values are at points 15 & 16?  The **75th percentile** will be the median of the upper 30 data points (31-60).  Again, since the count of the upper 30 points is even, the median will be the average of the two data points in the middle of points 31-60, which wil"	1	0	1	4	3.5	2.5	Medicine	51bb42c45e980e0e00000024	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	D3E946EF1EA1F704A9074CB5F1A68E8D	6/14/2013 16:20	CommentThread	FALSE	FALSE	6	None	289

"This excerpt from the wiki page on Prevalence answers your question:> In epidemiology, the prevalence or prevalence proportion is the proportion of a population found to have a condition (typically a disease or a risk factor such as smoking or seat-belt use). It is arrived at by comparing the number of people found to have the condition with the total number of people studied, and is usually expressed as a fraction, as a percentage or as the number of cases per 10,000 or 100,000 people. \Point prevalence\"" is the proportion of a population that has the condition at a specific point in time. \""Period prevalence\"" is the proportion of a population that has the condition at some time during a given period (\""12-month prevalence\"", etc.), and includes people who already have the condition at the start of the study period as well as those who acquire it during that period."""	1	0	1	4	3.5	3	Medicine	51bbc43d5e980e1600000037	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	3CC1D7C4DFDB45A6636246BFED375DA3	6/15/2013 1:32	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	2	51bb7a025e980e160000002d	70

"I set up my problems in Excel to avoid this issue altogether. "Interesting debate regarding the normality of height. Let me pose the question differently to show that height (and many other measures) cannot be normally distributed, although it can be well approximated as normal. According to the normal distribution, there should be the same proportion of people above the mean as there are below. However, height is >0, whereas it has no maximum (although in reality there could be a limit). So, suppose the mean height is 1.6m, and 0.0001% of the population is 3.3m; if height is normally distributed, then 0.0001% of the population is -0.1m tall, which is not a valid value. The actual % is irrelevant, to the argument.In fact, if you think about the last slide on % response for feelings about math, this MAY be normal ONLY if the mean was 50% and the distribution was unimodal. If the mean isn't 50%, then the distribution is not normal, because no one can answer <0% or >100%.But in many cases, people treat the distributions as approximately normal, because it is sufficient to perform the statistics.To summarize, there's probably no population data that's truly normal, but many are approximately normal (or their means are approximately normal), which in itself is sufficient to describe the data and perform statistical tests."	1	0	0	4	4	3.5	Medicine	51bd07cfc33ac91200000036	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	CC13B2B3ED234750DA3711F1D9E40F17	6/16/2013 0:33	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51b80b26f359c41200000163	275

"<redacted>, your question is interesting. "Hello Barine, I calculated it first, the median then I calculated the value of the 75% after that 25% and finally I subtracted them. For example:Your table is:   Yes = 1: 37; No = 0: 13; Total=50.First: Median = 1 because you count each sample until you count 25, that's is the half of our samples amount so that's mean the sample 25 is 1.Second: now you know the median. we calculate 75% of 50 samples. that is 37,5 we round which is 38. we find the sample 38 that is 1. Then we calculate 25% of 50 samples. That is 12,5 we round to 13 and like before we find the sample 25 which is 1 too. "It appears as though you may be referring to quiz 5 - part 2.  That's the only IQR quiz problem I see in Unit 1.Step 1 - Arrange the numbers in ascending order (reverse of what is shown).-300, -15, -14, -11, **-5, -4,** -3, 0, 3, 4You don't need the median in this problem.  But, if you did, since there are 10 numbers (even), it would be the average of the 5th and 6th numbers.The 75th percentile is the median of the upper half of numbers (-4, -3, **0**, 3, 4). "Left skewed distribution is one where observations are not distributed symmetrically around the center but continue farther to the left than to the right of the center. So due to non-symmetric spread while median stays at center, extreme leftward values drag mean lower than median as extreme values have dominant influence on mean but none on median. The list 1,2,3,10,11,12 is not at all skewed but perfectly symmetric."	0	0	1	4	3.5	2.5	Medicine	51c0a9ef22429c16000000b3	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	6DDE284124D9C7A46CDFB863C344227B	6/18/2013 18:41	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51c08a3222429c160000009d	218

"The numerator for variance is the summation of ***all*** squared deviations.  That means if you have several points the same distance from the mean, each distance is squared and added to the summation.If you have this frequency table:x, Frequency10, 512, 6The mean is ((5 x 10) + (6 x 12)) / (5 + 6)= (50 + 72) / 11 = 122 / 11 = 11.091Denominator of Variance is n - 1 = (5 + 6) - 1 = 11 - 1 = 10Numerator of Variance is summation of all squared distances from mean= (((10 - 11.091)^2) x 5) + (((12 - 11.091)^2) x 6)= (((-1.091)^2) x 5) + (((0.91)^2) x 6)= (1.19 x 5) + (0.826 x 6) = 5.95 + 4.96 = 10.909Divide 10.909 by n - 1 to get Variance = 10.909 / 10 = 1.091Take the square root of the Variance to get standard deviationStd Dev = sqrt(1.091) = 1.044So, you can use this general approach when you have a frequency table.  I suggest setting it up in Excel and double-checking with a calculator and paper."	0	0	1	4	3.5	2.5	Medicine	51c0abb922429c12000000b9	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	D3E946EF1EA1F704A9074CB5F1A68E8D	6/18/2013 18:49	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51c0a37b22429c0a000000be	112

"These links might help you:http://www.statisticshowto.com/articles/how-to-find-an-interquartile-range-in-statistics/http://classroom.synonym.com/calculate-interquartile-range-2744.htmlKeep in mind that that if you have an odd number of data points, the median is simply the middle value.  If you have an even number of data points, the median is the AVERAGE of the middle pair of data points.For example, if your data set is1 2 3 4 5we have an odd number of samples, so the middle value, 3, is the median.If our sample is1 2 3 4 5 6we have an even number of samples, so we want to average the middle pair of numbers, in this case (3, 4). "Agreed, it seems like the ethics of available race choices does not mirror reality.  But for whatever reason, these researchers only wanted to know prevalence in white vs. not white.  Perhaps it was so they could do a simple odds ratio instead of a multi-level odds ratio.  So, even though Race is not really a binary variable, it is for the purposes of this study and that's how the researchers set it up.  In other words, they only recorded white vs. not white, so it is binary.  If they recorded black vs. not black, that would be binary.  If they recorded Asian vs. not Asian, that would be binary.  If they set it up as a multi-category variable with several races, then it would no longer be binary, but categorical instead.  It just depends on how they setup the data collection categories.Another example might be if they were studying diabetes in the Americas and the choices were North America - Yes or No, then that would be binary.  If the choices  were North America, Central America or South America, that would be categorical.You bring up an excellent point to keep in mind when designing studies!"	0	0	1	4	3.5	2.5	Medicine	51c0c14022429c0a000000d5	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	D3E946EF1EA1F704A9074CB5F1A68E8D	6/18/2013 20:21	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51c0bc4322429c0e000000d1	84

"To calculate standard deviation, you sum the squares of each data point's difference from the mean. In a typical distribution, there are some values above and some below the mean, and so the difference is positive for some values and negative for othersFor example, suppose our data was: 1, 3, 5The mean is 3, and the standard deviation is calculated as sqrt(((1-3)^2 + (3-3)^2 + (5-3)^2)/2) = sqrt ( (-2)^2 + (0)^2 + (2)^2)Now, it doesn't matter if we're squaring a positive or a negative number (because the squares of both -2 and +2 are 4, in the example) but taking square roots of negative numbers would lead to standard deviation being and imaginary number or complex number, which is not a good idea!Raj"	0	0	1	4	3	1.5	Medicine	51c147887b03b3160000004d	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	3CC1D7C4DFDB45A6636246BFED375DA3	6/19/2013 5:54	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51c05b7622429c0e00000092	46

"\Number needed to treat\"" is the inverse of an absolute rate difference. As the absolute rate difference is measured in events per person, NNT is measured in persons per event. For example, if I knew the rate difference between two treatments in a particular case to be 1% (or 1 event per 100 people), I know that I will have to treat 100 (=1/0.01) people on average to see 1 less event.Raj"""	0	0	1	4	3	1.5	Medicine	51c37ae0de47500a0000003b	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	3CC1D7C4DFDB45A6636246BFED375DA3	6/20/2013 21:57	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	1	51c2ebdfde47500e0000001d	61

"Suppose you had 5 people in a study, who had been followed for the study for 1, 1, 0.5, 3 and 5 years respectively, person-years of follow up would be 10.5 (=1+1+0.5+3+5). Think of it as the average number of years followed multiplied by the number of people followed (hence the units are person-years). Person-years is popular as a unit because observing one person for 50 years or 50 people for 1 year each would give you the same number of data points, so you should treat both cases as equivalent.Raj"	0	0	1	4	3	1.5	Medicine	51c37ea80b08f81600000002	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	3CC1D7C4DFDB45A6636246BFED375DA3	6/20/2013 22:14	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51c22ab8de47501600000004	56

"I think these are probably both correct. [Some people][1] say risk. [Others][2] rate. It just depends on the units. The inverse of the absolute difference in **rate** is 1/(events/person-time). That gives you person-time over events. If the rate difference is 0.01 heart attack/person-years, you need to treat 100 people for one year to see one more heart attack.The inverse of the absolute difference in **risk** is 1/(events/people). That gives you people/event.To illustrate, if the risk difference is 0.01 heart attacks/people, you need to treat 100 people to see 1 more heart attack. I think it's probably better to use the rate than risk if you have it so you can be more precise about what you're saying. Also, if you are asked this question by the professor, probably you should use what she said rather than what someone else wrote.  [1]: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/<phoneRedac>  [2]: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_needed_to_treat"	1	0	1	4	3.5	3.5	Medicine	51c39d280b08f81600000009	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	ACA9A71615B0D15B876EC79337303114	6/21/2013 0:24	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51c36af3de47501200000046	72

"I have thought about this. I would show how the nomenclature goes like this: the original ratio is Events per Person-Year (E/P-Y). Without regard to multiplying by 100 or 1000 (just to eliminate the decimal), the units remain the same. Then, finding the NNT is simply the reciprocal of that original ratio. So, E/P-Y becomes Person-Year per Event (P-Y/E). In the case given 2.4 events/person-year, when \flipped\"" becomes .42. Then, manipulating the decimal by a factor of 100 yields 42 person-years per(one)event (P-Y/E).Therefore, the Event becomes the denominator when seeking the NNT.Also, take care to notice the \""dash\"" between Person and Year, i.e., Person-Year. This \""dash\"" implies Multiplication of the two dimensions. Similar to the physics measurement of torque is Foot-Pounds, or Newton-Kilograms. The \""dash\"" represents products of two dissimilar dimensions."""	1	0	0	4	3.5	2	Medicine	51c4ec1758b3d91600000009	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	8863D34E6D044E7016D307E116D852E1	6/22/2013 0:13	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51c4678b0b08f81600000036	100

"Rajhansa's definition can be more generalized to state that any variable where there are 'many' categories can be treated as continuous - it doesn't have to be very large (eg. all decimal numbers between 0-1 form a continuous range of numbers). How many is 'many' could be debatable. Perhaps what's more important is that to treat a discrete variable as continuous in a way that makes sense, it should be ordinal and the difference between adjacent classes should be identical in value. Eg. even though the age groupings (0-10, 10-20, 20-30, ... ) and (0-10, 10-30, 30-40, ...) are discrete, the former can be more easily treated as continuous than the latter."	1	0	0	4	3.5	2	Medicine	51c647ea9ab74c0a0000000c	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	CC13B2B3ED234750DA3711F1D9E40F17	6/23/2013 0:57	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51b87fd44983c00e00000031	184

"Well, if I get it right, when you do the simulation, you do *not* program the SEM.   All you program is the mean and the SD, and then take multiple samples. The distribution of the means of the simulated samples turns out to have a SEM about equal to SD/sqrt(n), but you did not tell the computer that! "Hi! I think it is not a matter of dose, but of number of pills. We assume that all combinations of pills contain the needed dose. In other words, the single pill and the 3 pills combinations have the same amount of drug, but the lower amount of pills make it easier for the patients. Thus, the patients with only one pill to take have higher levels of adherence (they take their medicine when they have to). This causes a better health and lower levels of hospitalization.This is why nowadays physicians tend to administrate, when possible, drug regimes that include the fewer pills as possible (this was not possible years ago, when HIV infected people had to take up to 30 pills per day)."	1	0	1	4	3.5	2	Medicine	51c856003927210e00000028	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	4AFBB02F6762718A8DF1E664A97815F3	6/24/2013 14:21	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51c759089ab74c0e00000038	398

"Hi,Observational studies may contain confounding factors. If one makes adjustments to take care of confounding, the resultant risk ratio is an Adjusted ratio else it's Unadjusted.More explanation - In most of our studies, we want to assess the impact of a treatment on a disease. In observational studies, we can't be sure whether the effect is due to our treatment or other confounding factors. So, investigators use  certain statistical model (logistic regression) to eliminate confounding. One can get the odd ratio adjusted for confounding using regression. Adjusted risk ratio can in turn be obtained from adjusted odds ratio.Hope this helps."	1	0	1	4	3.5	2	Medicine	51c891df3927211600000035	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	12313178C55E2DDF3A28A83E84D890B7	6/24/2013 18:37	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	2	51c871163927210a0000002f	184

"Hi cieursz. If you follow these groups of patients in time, then you can talk about cohorts. If you are collecting the data as the study evolves, it is prospective (also, if you examine the patients repeatingly in time, you can also call the study \longitudinal\""). If you use medical records from a series of patients, you might have a retrospective cohort.Please note that in a case-control study you start by picking patients who have already developed the outcome that you are investigating. In any case, since patients choose by themselves whether they take the intervention under study, I would suggest that your study is observational in nature. "That's an interesting notion! In such a situation, you potentially **could** use Bayes' theorem. Here's a simple example:Let's say we know that one of A, B, C, and D have a disease. The probability for each is equal to 0.25. If we test the pool of A & B's blood, and the test is negative for the disease, you can apply Bayes' theorem and update the probabilities of A & B having the disease to 0. Similarly, if we test C & D's blood, and the test is positive, the probabilities of each of C & D having the disease becomes 0.5. You can then perform a test on C. If it's positive, C has the disease. If not, D has the disease. You have essentially reached the result with 3 disease tests, whereas the naive approach of testing each person's blood separately would take 4 tests.Raj"	0	0	1	5	3	1	Medicine	51cbdc588deca61100000009	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	3CC1D7C4DFDB45A6636246BFED375DA3	6/27/2013 6:31	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	1	51ca9918d8b1a81200000019	103

"AjiPaul, your calculation is arithmetically correct, but as the professor states around 2:10, you can't actually calculate the risk ratio from the data in a case control study. The reason is because when do a case control study, you are manipulating the disease risk in your study. Imagine instead of choosing 50 patients with stroke and 50 without stroke, you chose 50 patients with stroke and 500 without stroke. Assuming that 4% of those who did not have stroke were smokers, then you get the following table. ```----------|smoker|non-smoker|  stroke----|----15|--------35|  no stroke-|----80|-------420|```  By extension, your RR would be (15/95) / (35/455) = 2.05, not 1.4.On the other hand, the OR is 2.25 no matter how many stroke and non-stroke patients you choose.Does that make sense?"	0	0	1	4	3	2	Medicine	51cbe97a8deca6110000000c	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	ACA9A71615B0D15B876EC79337303114	6/27/2013 7:27	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	1	51cb8e538deca61100000001	135

"BY my friend Gordon Doig a Biostatistician1. (A) Check to make sure authors report how allocation concealment was maintained. Trials that fail to report how allocation concealment was maintained tend to over-estimate treatment effect by up to 40%. If the trial did NOT maintain allocation concealment, save yourself time by throwing it out.2. (B) Did the authors use some form of blinding? Trials that do not use ANY form of blinding may over-estimate treatment effects by up to 26%.3. (C) Check for complete follow-up. If the trial is ICU based, if more than 10% of outcomes are not reported, throw the trial out. If the trial is not ICU based, or requires long follow-up outside the ICU and 20% of outcomes are missing, throw the trial out.4. Make sure you are not being misled by creative subgroup analyses:     - subgroup analyses should be defined in advanced     - the fewer, the better     - subgroup analyses MUST be based on factors that are identifiable at time of enrolment     - statistics MUST be based on tests of interaction OR discounted for multiple comparison5. Do not be mis-led by 'Cox Proportional Hazards' survival analysis. It assesses survival TIME, not the number of survivors at a set time.6. Assessment of baseline balance is more complex than just looking at baseline balance in Table 1. If something LOOKS like it is imbalanced, the authors can prove whether it influences conclusions by considering it in a covariate adjusted analysis. So, why not be liberal and consider almost all Table 1 variables?7. It is not a crime to change your primary outcome half way through a trial, as long as the decision is made without snooping on interim results.8. Snooping on interim results is cheating, unless you have pre-specified stopping rules. Stopping early is not cheating, if you follow your pre-specified stopping rules.9. Some industry funded trials are bad. Some academic trials are bad. If they adhere to the above 8 rules, there is a considerably lower chance of being 'bad'.10. Good journals publish bad trials and bad journals publish good trials. See rules 1 through 9 above.Gordps - sorry, those twitter ones were so bad I couldn't resist...."	1	0	0	4	4	2	Medicine	51cd23949b6a1b0e0000000d	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	65A1D8A2220ABD82B005C4A06ED32213	6/28/2013 5:48	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51cd04039b6a1b1600000008	64

"NNH is simply **defined** as using the reciprocal of the rate difference. That's all you needed to know for the homework. Watch the first minute of Unit 2 Module 3.If you're struggling to make sense of why it is defined as such: the year component of a person-year is relevant only to the length of the followups performed during the study. It's to account for cases where some members of the population are observed for different lengths of time.\The number needed to harm (NNH) is an epidemiological measure that indicates how many patients need to be exposed to a risk-factor over *a specific period* to cause harm in one patient that would not otherwise have been harmed\"" -from the same wiki article you linked.It's not like giving 30 people a medicine and instantly 1 person gets sick, it's over the same amount of observed time in the study. If the observation period was doubled, the rate difference would be doubled and subsequently the NNH would be halved."""	1	0	0	4	3.5	2	Medicine	51d07a7cae53041600000029	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	1082D7A2BDB0D98FF63A269E8A43AFE1	6/30/2013 18:35	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51c9da2297d0ab1200000060	97

If you want to know the number of events (as a proportion)within two particular points then you determine the AUC to know that. For eg if you integrate between 1 and 2 if the probability of something happening is in the form y=e^-x then the area of the integral between 1 and 2 represents the total number of people (or events as a proportion that took the values between 1 and 2.As an example take the normal curve  and alter the bars and you are getting the AUC which represents the proportion of events occurring (or values etc whatever you fixed as x and as an outcome y).This is true for any definite integralfor any equation which is continuous in the area of integration.	1	0	1	4	3.5	2	Medicine	51d0e36dae53040e00000041	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	65A1D8A2220ABD82B005C4A06ED32213	7/1/2013 2:03	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	0	51d0316eae53040e0000001d	82

"The definition of false positive is skewed in this problem. If I am responder and I fail the test (respond to the medication) then it is a positive test. "Very interesting posts, SusanC.Regarding your first post, you can have overlapping CIs and yet statistically significant p-values, there's no problem there (at least not necessarily!)Regarding your second post, GLIMMIX stands for generalized linear mixed models. \Generalized linear\"" because the outcome in your case is apparently dichotomous, or maybe polytomous (hence the \""logistic\"" part and the ORs as results). The \""mixed\"" part is to account for the correlation in the data, since they come from repeated measures on the same patients (the study is \""longitudinal\""). The whole \""mixed models\"" stuff has been a hot topic in biostats for at least a decade now. Its conception goes way back in time of course, but with software advances its use is now beginning to spread in clinical journals. It allows a lot more flexibility than traditional methods, so be prepared to see a *lot* more of those models in the near future. This is certainly so for \""linear mixed models\"" for continuous outcomes, but I guess their \""generalized\"" cousins for other types of outcomes are making progress fast. Needless to say, one must know how to handle this stuff, and I'm not sure what \""guarantees\"" a reviewer should ask to ensure proper use. It's a topic worth of some on-line search!Now, regarding the small values of the coefficients, this is probably due to the tiny units of measurement (*micromoles*, right?), as Kristin has pointed above. Remember that a regression coefficient reflects changes for a *unit* difference in the corresponding predictor.The gem of the posts, of course, is the apparent CI/p-value discrepancy for regression-estimated odds ratios. This is something that has happened to me when running standard logistic regression (not the \""mixed\"" variety that you mention). I was also incredulous at first, until some search showed that they are calculated using different approximations! I'd think that something similar applies in this case also. For more details, see for example this link, I think you will find it enlightening:http://www.epietalum.net/content/p0001-ci-085-731-or-how-can-confidence-interval-risk-ratio-include-1-if-p-value-0001So, my message is this: cheer up, all hope is not lost!"""	0	0	1	4	3.5	2	Medicine	51d2eb7ebbdc2e160000001c	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	191338A927E00DB06D80859748977BA3	7/2/2013 15:02	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	1	51d07c79ae53040e0000002a	106

"I really have to take issue with Unit3 Homework question 4, because for the \correct\"" answer suggested (0.33), the question is simply and plainly worded WRONGLY.  For the answer to be 33% the question should say \""What is the probability that she will survive the NEXT 5 years ... to reach ten years.\""   I normally would not consider myself to have any problem writing or reading English.By drawing out an event tree I quite easily worked out the intermediate probability and had it in my hand but pondered long and hard about what the question was asking for and bizarre as it may have seemed to me, the question was quite plain -- it said \""WHAT IS THE PROBABILITY THAT SHE WILL SURVIVE 10 YEARS.\""  Well, that is quite clear. "I like to think about independence like this: If two events A & B are independent, if I tell you whether A occurred or not, that will not allow you to update the probability of B occurring. Here's a simple example: Suppose A is rolling a die and getting 6, and B is it raining in Stanford tomorrow. If I tell you that A occurred, that doesn't give you any additional information to predict whether it will rain in Stanford tomorrow! Thus, A & B are independent.But if I tell you that A has occurred, you can say with certainty that ~A has NOT occurred. Similarly, if A has not occurred, you can say with certainty that ~A HAS occurred. Thus, A & ~A cannot be independent.Raj"	0	0	1	4	3	1	Medicine	51d3a0f1bbdc2e1200000064	Medicine/HRP258/Statistics_in_Medicine	3CC1D7C4DFDB45A6636246BFED375DA3	7/3/2013 3:56	Comment	FALSE	FALSE	1	51d11c9ff7b9500e00000008	90

"Sensitivity & Specificity tell about the patients who have not yet undergone the test . So **before doing actual test** , given that patient is non-responder to antibiotic, what's the chance the patient tests positive : **senstivity** ; and **before doing actual test** , given that patient is responder to antibiotic, what's the chance the patient tests negative : **specificity** . On the other hand PPV & NPV tell us about the patients who have undergone the actual test . So **post testing** , given that patient tests positive, what's the chance that the patient is drug resistant : **PPV**. Similarly **post testing** , given that patient tests negative, what's the chance that the patient is drug sensitive : **NPV** . "You could write out the expected number of tests it would take as a function of prevalence, group size, and size of total population. So for example, if prevalence is 'p', group size is 'x' and total population is 'T', the expected number of tests would be:E(# tests)= T/x* ( 1*(1-p)^x + (x+1)*(1-(1-p)^x))(You can figure out where this came from, from Prof. <redacted>'s example in the video)Now, you need to minimize the expected number of tests, and the only thing you can control is x, because p and T are set for you. "The lecturer states: \Essentially, conceptually, p values give you the probability that the observed effect could have arisen by chance\"".  This can be confusing.  She might have said more accurately \""conceptually, p values give you the probability that the observed effect could have arisen if the null hypothesis were true\"" which is what she did say in the sentence before. There should be an underlying assumption that the result (and any result) is chance and the p value measures the probability of that chance finding if the null hypothesis were true, ie what are the chances of getting that finding if the null hypothesis is true not what is the chance the finding arose by chance.  The p value can't measure the probability of it being a chance finding but rather the chance of the finding given the null hypothesis. If the value seems too extreme then you either 1)reject the null hypothesis or 2)conjecture that you have witnessed a very low probability event. This is a very important distinction.
